tamil:
மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும் பார்ப்பான்
பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Marappinum oththuk kolalaagum paarppaan
Pirappozhukkam kundrak kedum.
current_meaning: A Brahmin (a member of the priestly class) who forgets the Vedas (holy texts) can learn them again. But if he loses the good behaviour of his birth, his birth itself is ruined.
elementary: If you forget your spelling words, you can study them again. But if you become a bully, no amount of studying fixes that. You lose something that is much harder to get back.
university: This couplet is the chapter's sharpest test case. The paarppaan (Brahmin) is the figure whose status depends most on birth and learning. Valluvar concedes that forgotten Vedic learning (oththu) can be recovered, but if pirappozhukkam, the conduct attached to that birth, declines (kundra), the birth itself is ruined (kedum). The logic is asymmetric: knowledge is a stock that can be replenished, while character is a foundation whose collapse brings down everything built on it. Commentators split between reading the couplet as upholding Brahmin duty (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) and as ranking birth below conduct (Karunanidhi). It closely echoes Manu 1.109, where a Brahmin who departs from the rule of conduct ‘does not reap the fruit of the Veda’, and Yudhishthira's answer to the Yaksha in the Mahabharata.

tamil:
அழுக்கா றுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம்போன்று இல்லை
ஒழுக்க மிலான்கண் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaan-kan aakkampoandru illai
Ozhukkam ilaan-kan uyarvu.
current_meaning: Just as riches never stay with jealous people, greatness never comes to people without good behaviour.
elementary: A jealous kid spends so much time being upset about what others have that he never enjoys his own things. In the same way, someone who behaves badly never really rises high, no matter what.
university: The couplet works by analogy (ponru, ‘just as’). Azhukkaaru, envy, is so incompatible with aakkam (increase, prosperity) that its absence is proverbial, and uyarvu (elevation, rank) is just as surely absent from a person without ozhukkam. Envy gets a whole later chapter (17). Pappaiah reads uyarvu as ‘high lineage’, keeping the chapter's theme of birth, while Varadarasanar reads it as elevation in life generally. The pairing of envy with misconduct is deliberate: Tamil ethics treats envy as the model inner corruption that eats away at outward fortune, which a later couplet (Kural 168) develops. The claim is about incompatibility more than reward: certain dispositions cannot coexist with certain goods.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் ஒல்கார் உரவோர் இழுக்கத்தின்
ஏதம் படுபாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin olgaar uravoar izhukkaththin
Edham padupaak karindhu.
current_meaning: Strong-minded people never slip in their behaviour, because they know the trouble a slip brings.
elementary: A smart bike rider always wears a helmet, not because they are scared, but because they know how badly a fall can hurt. Strong people keep behaving well for the same reason: they know what happens when you don't.
university: Uravor, ‘the strong’, refers to strength of mind rather than of body (uram means firmness or resolve). Their steadiness is not naive. It rests on knowing (arindhu) the edham (fault, harm, calamity) that falls on those who lapse. That makes the couplet an argument about moral knowledge: firmness comes from seeing consequences clearly. Olkaar (‘they do not bend or slacken’) suggests constant, everyday vigilance rather than heroic resistance to one temptation. Pappaiah adds that they hold on ‘even when it is hard’ and reads the harm as loss of standing. Many traditions picture true strength as self-mastery: Ben Zoma's ‘Who is mighty?’, the Buddhist rock unshaken by the storm, and Odysseus binding himself because he knows what the Sirens do.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் எய்துவர் மேன்மை இழுக்கத்தின்
எய்துவர் எய்தாப் பழி.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai izhukkaththin
Eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi.
current_meaning: Through good behaviour people become great. Through bad behaviour they earn a shame they never needed to suffer.
elementary: When you are kind and honest, people look up to you. When you cheat or lie, you get a bad name, and it is a bad name you could easily have avoided.
university: The couplet is built as a strict parallel: ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai / izhukkaththin eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi, ‘by conduct they attain eminence; by lapse they attain unattainable blame’. The paradoxical phrase eydhaap pazhi (‘blame that should not be attained’) is read in different ways: as undeserved, as unbearable, or as blame one had no need to incur. Pope's ‘censures undeserved’ takes the first reading, and most modern commentators take the last. Either way, the couplet makes the social stakes of conduct explicit, because menmai (eminence) and pazhi (blame) are verdicts passed by others. Here the chapter moves from inner firmness (136) to public consequence. The same pairing appears in Sanskrit dharmashastra, in the rabbinic ‘crown of a good name’, and in Hesiod's steep path to excellence.

tamil:
நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம் தீயொழுக்கம்
என்றும் இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Nandrikku viththaagum nallozhukkam theeyozhukkam
Endrum idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Good behaviour is the seed of good things. Bad behaviour always brings sorrow.
elementary: Plant an apple seed and you get an apple tree. Plant weeds and you get weeds. Being good is like planting a good seed, because nice things grow from it. Being mean only grows trouble.
university: The farming metaphor vittu (seed) makes nallozhukkam generative. Good conduct is not the good itself but the cause from which good (nandri, here ‘benefit’ or ‘virtue’ rather than ‘gratitude’, though one modern commentator reads it that way) grows over time. Its opposite, theeyozhukkam, gives idumbai (distress) endrum, ‘always’, which suggests a continuous harvest rather than a single punishment. Pappaiah extends the fruit to this life and the next (immai, marumai), which aligns the couplet with karmic causation, while Karunanidhi keeps it within this life. The seed image is nearly universal, from Paul's ‘whatsoever a man soweth’ to the Upanishadic ‘as he acts, so he becomes’ and Aristotle's view that character arises from like activities.

tamil:
ஒழுக்க முடையவர்க்கு ஒல்லாவே தீய
வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaiyavarkku ollaave theeya
Vazhukkiyum vaayaal solal.
current_meaning: People with good behaviour cannot speak bad words, not even by mistake.
elementary: Some people are so used to being kind that even when they are angry or surprised, mean words just don't come out. Being good becomes so natural that it even protects your mouth.
university: The key word is vazhukkiyum, ‘even when slipping’ or ‘even by inadvertence’. Valluvar does not say the disciplined hold back evil speech by effort. He says it is ollaa for them, impossible or unfitting: conduct has become so much second nature that even an unguarded moment is safe. This is a strong claim about habituation, close to Aristotle's view that the virtuous person does the right thing with pleasure and without inner struggle. Tamil ethics gives speech special attention, with chapters on sweet speech (10) and on avoiding useless speech (20). Parallel traditions do too: the Gita counts truthful, non-distressing speech as an austerity, rabbinic ethics condemns lashon hara, and Buddhism places right speech on the Eightfold Path.

tamil:
உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் பலகற்றும்
கல்லார் அறிவிலா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal pala-katrum
Kallaar arivilaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who have not learned to live well with the world are foolish, no matter how many books they have read.
elementary: Someone could read every book in the library, but if they cannot get along with people, share, or be polite, they have not really learned the most important lesson.
university: The chapter closes on a paradox: pala-katrum kallaar, ‘having learned much, they have not learned’. What they lack is ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal, conduct that ‘sticks to’ or fits with the world. Commentators differ on what ‘the world’ means. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar take it as the worthy (uyarndhor). Pappaiah boldly reads it as adapting the old ethical texts to present circumstances and dropping what no longer fits, which turns the couplet into almost a charter for moral reasoning over rote rule-following. On any reading, social wisdom is the test of learning. This echoes the rabbinic principle that derech eretz (right conduct) comes before Torah, and Aristotle's scorn for people who ‘take refuge in theory’.

tamil:
பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை ஞாலத்து
அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Piranporulaal pettozhugum pedhaimai gnaalaththu,
Aramporul kandaarkan il.
current_meaning: People who truly understand right and wrong, and how the world works, are never so foolish as to desire another man’s wife.
elementary: Imagine someone who has studied all the rules of a game very carefully. That person would never try to grab another player's pieces, because they understand how the game works and why the rules matter. This kural says people who really understand what is right and good would never want someone else's husband or wife.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by framing adultery first as a failure of intelligence (பேதைமை, 'folly') rather than simply as a sin. The phrase அறம்பொருள் கண்டார் — 'those who have seen aram and porul' — deliberately invokes the first two aims of life that structure the Kural itself (virtue and worldly prosperity), implying that a person who grasps either domain properly would recognise such desire as self-defeating. The word பொருளாள் ('she who is another's porul') reflects the social vocabulary of its age, in which a wife was spoken of as belonging within another's household; modern readers often recast it as a violation of another's committed bond. The kural thus locates the root of the wrong in ignorance, a move that parallels Socratic and Buddhist views that wrongdoing flows from failed understanding.

tamil:
அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம் பிறன்கடை
நின்றாரின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Arankadai nindraarul ellaam pirankadai,
Nindraarin pedhaiyaar il.
current_meaning: Of all people who do wrong, no one is a bigger fool than the man who stands at another man’s door, wanting his wife.
elementary: Think of all the silly, wrong things people can do. This kural says that out of all of them, the silliest is waiting outside a neighbour's house because you want the person who belongs to that family. It is the worst kind of wrong choice.
university: The couplet turns on a pun with the word கடை, which can mean both 'the outermost/lowest point' and 'a gate or doorway': அறன்கடை ('beyond the edge of virtue') is set against பிறன்கடை ('at another's gate'). Valluvar thus ranks wrongdoers and places the would-be adulterer, loitering at a neighbour's door, at the very bottom for sheer foolishness. The image of standing at the gate stresses both the humiliation of the act and its risk: the man is exposed, waiting, and dependent on another's household. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read this as a claim that even among sinners this particular vice is uniquely irrational, because it brings danger without any lasting gain.

tamil:
விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் மன்ற தெளிந்தாரில்
தீமை புரிந்துதொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Vilindhaarin verallar mandra thelindhaaril,
Theemai purindhozhugu vaar.
current_meaning: People who do wrong with the wife of a friend who trusts them completely are surely no better than dead.
elementary: Suppose a friend trusts you so much that they let you into their home anytime. If you used that trust to try to take what is most precious to their family, you would be like a broken, empty person inside, with nothing good left alive in you. That is what this kural says.
university: The key word தெளிந்தார் means 'those who are clear' or 'those who trust without suspicion': the victims here are friends who have let the man into their home precisely because they do not doubt him. Valluvar's verdict, விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் ('not different from the dead'), is a moral rather than literal death: the betrayer has extinguished what makes a person trustworthy and therefore socially alive. Commentators note the intensifier மன்ற ('certainly'), which removes any softening. The couplet thus adds betrayal of trust to the chapter's charge of folly, anticipating the ancient idea, shared by Stoics and scriptural traditions, that faithlessness destroys the essence of a human being.

tamil:
எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம் தினைத்துணையும்
தேரான் பிறனில் புகல்.
transliteration:
Enaiththunaiyar aayinum ennaam thinaiththunaiyum,
Theraan piranil pugal.
current_meaning: However great a man may be, what is his greatness worth if he goes after another man’s wife without thinking even a little about how wrong it is?
elementary: Imagine the best player on a team, who is famous and loved by everyone. If that player cheated in a very unfair way without stopping to think, all their fame would be worth nothing. This kural says the same about a person who goes after someone else's husband or wife: being important cannot save them.
university: The couplet plays two measures against each other: எனைத்துணை ('however great a measure') and தினைத்துணை ('a millet grain's measure'), the smallest unit in Tamil idiom. A man may possess vast greatness, yet if he does not reflect (தேரான்) for even a millet grain's worth before entering another's home, that greatness is worthless. The rhetorical question என்னாம் ('what does it become?') leaves the answer, nothing, to the listener. The emphasis on failing to reflect links to the chapter's theme of folly: the danger lies in the thoughtless moment in which rank and reputation are thrown away, a pattern visible in stories of kings and heroes across many cultures.

tamil:
எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான் எய்துமெஞ் ஞான்றும்
விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி.
transliteration:
Elidhena illirappaan eydhum enjnjaandrum,
Viliyaadhu nirkum pazhi.
current_meaning: A man who goes after another man’s wife, thinking it is easy, earns a shame that never dies and stays with him forever.
elementary: Some mistakes are like writing on sand: they wash away. Others are like carving into stone: they stay forever. This kural says that going after someone else's husband or wife might seem easy at the time, but the shame is carved in stone and never goes away.
university: Valluvar contrasts the ease of the act (எளிது, 'easy') with the permanence of its consequence (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி, 'blame that stands undying'). The verb இல்லிறப்பான் combines இல் ('home') and இறப்பு ('crossing over, transgressing'), so the offender is literally 'one who oversteps a home'. The couplet reflects a culture where reputation (புகழ்) was treated as the only thing that outlives a person, a theme developed in the Kural's later chapter on fame; adultery produces the exact opposite, a lasting infamy. The asymmetry between a moment's ease and an eternity of blame is a common moral argument, found in scriptural warnings about reproach that 'shall not be wiped away'.

tamil:
பகைபாவம் அச்சம் பழியென நான்கும்
இகவாவாம் இல்லிறப்பான் கண்.
transliteration:
Pagaipaavam achcham pazhiyena naangum,
Igavaavaam illirappaan kan.
current_meaning: Hatred, sin, fear and shame: these four never leave a man who wrongs another man’s home.
elementary: Picture someone who takes a thing that belongs to another family. Now four shadows follow them everywhere: people are angry at them, they know they did wrong, they are always scared of being caught, and others think badly of them. This kural says those four shadows never go away.
university: This couplet is a compact catalogue: பகை (enmity from the wronged husband and his kin), பாவம் (sin, the moral or karmic stain), அச்சம் (constant fear of discovery and revenge), and பழி (public blame). The verb இகவா ('they do not depart') makes all four permanent companions. The list covers the social, spiritual, psychological, and reputational costs of the act, a strikingly complete analysis for two lines. Its closest parallel is Dhammapada 309, which also names exactly four misfortunes for the man who goes to another's wife, a resemblance that scholars have noted when discussing shared ethical currents in early South Asian literature.

tamil:
அறனியலான் இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் பிறனியலாள்
பெண்மை நயவா தவன்.
transliteration:
Araniyalaan ilvaazhvaan enbaan piraniyalaal,
Penmai nayavaa thavan.
current_meaning: A man who does not desire a woman who belongs to another is the one called a true family man, living the right way.
elementary: What makes someone a good member of a family? This kural gives a simple test: a good family person is happy with their own family and never wishes for someone else's husband or wife. Being loyal is part of being good at home.
university: Here Valluvar turns from warning to definition: the true இல்வாழ்வான் (householder), the central figure of the whole இல்லறவியல் section, is identified by a negative mark, not desiring பிறனியலாள் ('she who moves within another's sphere'). The word இயல் appears twice, linking அறன்இயலான் ('one whose conduct is shaped by virtue') to பிறன்இயலாள் ('one whose life is joined to another'), so the couplet balances two kinds of belonging. By defining domestic virtue through fidelity, the Kural treats chastity as a duty of husbands as much as of wives, which some modern commentators highlight as notably even-handed for its era. The idea that the good household is built on the spouse's exclusive devotion appears in many traditions' ideals of marriage.

tamil:
பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை சான்றோர்க்கு
அறனொன்றோ ஆன்ற வொழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Piranmanai nokkaadha peraanmai saandrorkku,
Aranondro aandra ozhukku.
current_meaning: For good people, the great courage of not even looking at another man’s wife with desire is not just goodness. It is the fullness of right living.
elementary: Being truly strong is not about big muscles. This kural says real strength is choosing not even to look at someone else's husband or wife in a wanting way. That kind of self-control is the strongest and best way to behave.
university: The striking term பேராண்மை ('great manliness' or 'supreme valour') redefines heroism: in a culture that prized martial courage, Valluvar says the greatest valour is the self-mastery not to look (நோக்காத) at another's wife with desire. The couplet moves the moral line from the act to the gaze, the same shift found in the Sermon on the Mount and in the Qur'anic command to lower the gaze. The second line says this restraint is not just one virtue (அறன் ஒன்றோ, 'is it only virtue?') but ஆன்ற ஒழுக்கு, complete or mature conduct, linking this chapter back to the preceding chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (right conduct). For the சான்றோர் (the noble or accomplished), then, this restraint is the crown of character.

tamil:
நலக்குரியார் யாரெனின் நாமநீர் வைப்பின்
பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள்தோயா தார்.
transliteration:
Nalakkuriyaar yaarenin naamaneer vaippin,
Pirarkkuriyaal tholthoyaa thaar.
current_meaning: In this world circled by the fearsome sea, who truly deserves every good thing? Those who do not touch a woman who belongs to another man.
elementary: If you asked, 'Who deserves all the best things in the whole wide world?', this kural has an answer: the people who stay loyal and never go after someone else's husband or wife. Being faithful makes you worthy of good things.
university: The couplet is framed as a question and answer, a device Valluvar uses to give his verdict extra force. The phrase நாமநீர் வைப்பு ('the world set within fearsome waters') is a classical Tamil epithet for the earth encircled by the ocean, so the claim is universal: anywhere in the world. The one worthy of நலம் (goodness, blessing, well-being) is identified by a concrete image, தோள் தோயாதார் ('those whose shoulders do not touch'), an embrace withheld. After several couplets on the ruin that follows adultery, this one reverses the angle and promises reward, showing that the chapter aims to encourage as well as warn.

tamil:
அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் பிறன்வரையாள்
பெண்மை நயவாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Aranvaraiyaan alla seyinum piranvaraiyaal,
Penmai nayavaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even if a man does not live by what is right and does many wrong things, it is still good if he does not desire another man’s wife.
elementary: Imagine someone who breaks lots of rules. This kural says: even if they have not been good at many things, they should at least keep this one rule and never go after someone else's husband or wife. It is the one line everyone must never cross.
university: The closing couplet makes a realistic concession: even a man who does not stay within virtue's limits (அறன் வரையான்) and does what should not be done (அல்ல செயினும்) should at least not desire one who lives within another's limits (பிறன் வரையாள்). The repetition of வரை ('boundary') creates a pointed wordplay: he may cross the bounds of virtue, but must not cross the bounds of another's marriage. By holding this line even for the imperfect, Valluvar marks adultery as a floor below which no one should fall, not merely an ideal for saints. The move is pastoral as well as moral, offering even the flawed a place to begin.

tamil:
அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை
இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை.
transliteration:
Agazhvaaraith thaangum nilampoalath thammai,
Igazhvaarp poruththal thalai.
current_meaning: The ground holds up even the people who dig into it. In the same way, the best thing you can do is calmly put up with people who insult you and look down on you.
elementary: Think about the ground under your feet. People dig holes in it, stomp on it and poke it with shovels, and it still holds everybody up without complaining. This kural says the best kind of person is like that ground: when someone is mean to you, you stay steady and kind instead of hitting back.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with one of the most famous images in Tamil ethics: the earth (நிலம்) that supports the very people who dig into it (அகழ்வார்). The two verbs are set side by side on purpose. அகழ் (to dig, to wound the ground) matches இகழ் (to scorn, to wound with words), so an insult is pictured as digging into a person, and the patient person takes it in the way soil does, without caving in. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah point out that the earth doesn't just put up with the digger; it keeps holding him up so he doesn't fall, which makes endurance an active kind of support. The last word, தலை ('the foremost'), puts forbearance at the head of the virtues and sets up the thesis the rest of the chapter develops. Other traditions reach for the same metaphor: the Sanskrit kṣamā means both 'earth' and 'forgiveness,' and the Buddha compares abusive speech to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe.

tamil:
பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை
மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று.
transliteration:
Poruththal irappinai endrum adhanai,
Maraththal adhaninum nandru.
current_meaning: Always put up with the wrongs people do to you, even when they go too far. Forgetting those wrongs completely is even better.
elementary: If a friend breaks your favorite toy, being patient about it is good. This kural says something is even better: letting it go so completely that you stop thinking about it. Holding onto a hurt is like carrying a heavy rock in your pocket, and forgetting it is like finally throwing the rock away.
university: The couplet sets up two steps: பொறுத்தல் (bearing a wrong) and, higher still, மறத்தல் (forgetting it). The key word இறப்பு here means 'transgression, going beyond bounds.' Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagan and Mu. Varadarasan read it as an excessive wrong, not as 'death,' although some popular modern glosses take it as 'until death.' Valluvar's point is psychological: if you endure a wrong but still keep a record of it, the endurance is incomplete, because the remembered wrong keeps feeding resentment. Real forbearance lets the grievance go altogether. Rabbinic law draws a similar line between taking vengeance and bearing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18, discussed in Talmud Yoma 23a), and Nietzsche later observed that some strong natures 'forgive' simply by forgetting.

tamil:
இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால் வன்மையுள்
வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Inmaiyul inmai virundhoraal vanmaiyul,
Vanmai madavaarp porai.
current_meaning: The worst kind of being poor is having nothing to offer a guest. The greatest kind of strength is staying patient with foolish people.
elementary: Being poor isn't only about having little money. This kural says the saddest kind of poor is not being able to share even a snack with a friend who visits. Being strong isn't only about big muscles either: the strongest kind of strong is staying calm when someone acts silly or rude to you.
university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a double superlative, இன்மையுள் இன்மை ('the poverty within poverty') and வன்மையுள் வன்மை ('the strength within strength'), and uses it to pair two virtues that seem unrelated. The first half looks back to the chapter on hospitality (விருந்தோம்பல், ch. 9), where turning away a guest is the gravest failure of a household. The second half redefines might as the ability to bear the provocations of மடவார், 'the ignorant' or 'foolish.' Setting them side by side suggests a shared logic: hospitality and forbearance both measure inner abundance, not outward resources. Redefining strength as self-mastery is one of the most widely shared moral reversals across traditions, from the Mishnah's 'Who is mighty?' to the hadith about the strong man who controls his anger.

tamil:
நிறையுடைமை நீங்காமை வேண்டின் பொறையுடைமை
போற்றி யொழுகப் படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyudaimai neengaamai vendin poraiyudaimai,
Potri yozhugap padum.
current_meaning: If you never want to lose your good, steady character, you must value patience and live by it every day.
elementary: Imagine your good character is a glass filled to the top with water. Every time you lose your temper, some spills out. This kural says that if you want to keep your glass full, you have to carry it carefully, which means being patient all the time.
university: நிறை is a rich Tamil word meaning fullness, completeness, and also self-restraint or integrity. It describes a wife's guarded constancy in chapter 6 and the sages 'full of word' in chapter 3. Valluvar makes பொறையுடைமை (possessing patience) the precondition for keeping நிறையுடைமை (possessing fullness). The two '-உடைமை' compounds deliberately echo each other, which suggests patience is not one virtue among many but the container that keeps the others from leaking away. The phrase போற்றி ஒழுகுதல் ('to guard and live by') implies constant vigilance, not occasional restraint, and Solomon Pappaiah reads நிறை as சான்றாண்மை, the complete nobility of character treated in chapter 99. The Epistle of James makes almost the same claim, that patience is what makes a person 'perfect and entire.'

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையாரே வைப்பர்
பொறுத்தாரைப் பொன்போற் பொதிந்து.
transliteration:
Oruththaarai ondraaga vaiyaare vaippar,
Poruththaaraip ponpor podhindhu.
current_meaning: People think nothing of those who pay back every wrong. But they treasure those who stay patient, like gold kept safe and wrapped up.
elementary: Two kids get pushed in the lunch line. One shoves back hard, and the other says, 'It's okay.' Later, which one do people trust and want as a friend? This kural says people treasure the patient one like a piece of gold kept safe in a box, while the one who always hits back isn't valued at all.
university: ஒறுத்தார் ('those who punished' the offender) and பொறுத்தார் ('those who bore it') differ by a single initial consonant, and Valluvar uses the near-rhyme to make the moral contrast audible. ஒன்றாக வையார் means such people are not counted as anything at all, while பொன்போற் பொதிந்து வைப்பர் ('they wrap and keep like gold') suggests a treasure bundled up and stored with care. The judgement is a social one: honor goes not to the person who wins the exchange of blows but to the one who refuses it. That reverses a warrior-culture instinct that leaving a slight unavenged is shameful. Aristotle is a useful contrast: he praises the good-tempered man who 'tends to make allowances,' but warns that putting up with every insult can look 'slavish.' Valluvar settles that tension firmly on the side of forbearance.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம் பொறுத்தார்க்குப்
பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்.
transliteration:
Oruththaarkku orunaalai inbam poruththaarkkup,
Pondrun thunaiyum pugazh.
current_meaning: Getting even brings happiness for just one day. Staying patient brings praise that lasts as long as the world lasts.
elementary: Getting back at someone can feel good, for about one day. Then the good feeling is gone. Being the person who stayed kind is different: people remember it and talk about it for a very, very long time.
university: The couplet sets two time-scales against each other: ஒருநாளை இன்பம் ('one day's pleasure') and பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் ('fame until [the world] perishes'). Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah read பொன்றும் as the ending of the world, while Kalaignar reads it as 'throughout one's life.' Either way the basic contrast between passing gratification and lasting reputation holds. Valluvar is speaking the language of புகழ், the enduring renown he devotes chapter 24 to, where reputation is treated as the only thing that outlives the body. The psychological point is sharp: Aristotle also observes that revenge 'relieves' anger by 'producing ... pleasure instead of pain,' but Valluvar insists that this pleasure is the shortest-lived of goods.

tamil:
திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும் நோநொந்து
அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Thiranalla tharpirar seyyinum nononthu,
Aranalla seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even when others hurt you in ways you did not deserve, it is good to feel sorry for the pain their wrong will bring them, and not to do wrong back.
elementary: When someone is unfair to you, you might want to be unfair back. This kural says don't. Instead, feel a little sad for them, because doing wrong usually comes back to hurt the person who does it, and keep doing the right thing yourself.
university: The key phrase is நோநொந்து. Mu. Varadarasan reads it as grieving over the suffering (நோ) that will fall on the wrongdoer as the fruit of his act, which makes the couplet an ethic of compassion toward the offender rather than mere self-restraint. Solomon Pappaiah offers a slightly different nuance, grieving at the thought that retaliation would hurt him, but both readings end in refusing அறனல்ல, 'what is not dharma.' The couplet therefore goes beyond tolerance to a positive moral stance: being injured doesn't license you to abandon virtue. Socrates states the same principle in the Crito, that it is never right to return wrong for wrong, and Jesus acts it out on the cross by praying for those who crucify him.

tamil:
மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை செய்தாரைத் தாந்தம்
தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
transliteration:
Migudhiyaan mikkavai seydhaaraith thaandham,
Thagudhiyaan vendru vidal.
current_meaning: When proud people do you great wrongs because they think they are above you, beat them with your own goodness, which means your patience.
elementary: Sometimes a bully acts big and mean, and you might think the only way to win is to be even meaner. This kural says you can beat them another way: by staying calm and good. Your patience works like a superpower that makes their meanness look small.
university: The couplet plays on மிகுதி ('excess, arrogance') and தகுதி ('fitness, worth'). The aggressor acts out of surplus (மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை, 'excessive deeds out of excess'), and is to be overcome by the victim's own proper measure (தாந்தம் தகுதியான்). Commentators consistently identify this தகுதி with பொறை, patience itself, so forbearance becomes a strategy for victory rather than passive defeat. The verb, வென்று விடல் ('conquer'), is deliberately martial: Valluvar claims the vocabulary of winning for the person who doesn't retaliate. The same logic appears in Paul's 'overcome evil with good,' in the Qur'an's 'repel evil with what is better,' and in Vidura's maxim that anger is conquered by forgiveness, a maxim that reappears almost word for word in the Dhammapada (v. 223).

tamil:
துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை உடையர் இறந்தார்வாய்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarin thooimai udaiyar irandhaarvaai,
Innaachchol norkir pavar.
current_meaning: People who can calmly take the harsh words of those who go too far are as pure as those who have given up the world.
elementary: Monks and nuns who give up everything are often thought of as very pure. This kural says you don't have to leave home to be that pure. If someone yells nasty words at you and you stay calm, your heart is just as clean as theirs.
university: இறந்தார் here doesn't mean 'the dead.' It means 'those who have transgressed' (from இற, to go beyond), the same root as இறப்பு in Kural 152. Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar confirm this sense, though some popular glosses take it literally. The comparison with துறந்தார் ('renunciants') matters because these chapters belong to இல்லறவியல், the section on the householder's life: Valluvar claims that a householder who endures insult reaches the purity normally reserved for ascetics. Solomon Pappaiah makes this explicit, saying that even living a household life, such a person is as pure as a renunciant. The verb நோற்றல் ('to endure as an austerity') anticipates the next couplet's comparison with fasting and recasts patience itself as a form of tapas.

tamil:
உண்ணாது நோற்பார் பெரியர் பிறர்சொல்லும்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்.
transliteration:
Unnaadhu norpaar periyar pirarsollum,
Innaachchol norpaarin pin.
current_meaning: People who go without food to train themselves are great. But they come second to people who put up with the cruel words others say to them.
elementary: Going without food for a whole day to be good is really hard, and people admire it. This kural says something is even harder and better: when someone says mean things to you and you swallow your anger and stay kind, you are the real champion.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter by ranking two kinds of நோன்பு (austerity): உண்ணாது நோற்றல், enduring hunger by fasting, and இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல், enduring cruel speech. By placing the faster 'after' (பின்) the one who bears insult, he puts the most visible ascetic practice of his time, prominent in both Jain and Brahmanical asceticism, below an inner, social virtue. Repeating நோற்பார் in both lines insists that patience is itself tapas, completing the argument begun in Kural 159. The ranking resonates with the Dhammapada's 'Enduring patience is the highest austerity,' with the hadith that tells a fasting person to answer abuse by saying 'I am fasting,' and with Isaiah's prophetic critique that a true fast is measured by ethical conduct.

tamil:
ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க ஒருவன்தன் நெஞ்சத்து
அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaaraak kolga oruvanthan nenjathu
Azhukkaaru ilaadha iyalbu.
current_meaning: Make it a rule of your life to keep your heart free of jealousy.
elementary: Some families have house rules, like “always say please.” This kural says: make “never be jealous of anyone” one of your own rules, as important as any other rule for being good.
university: Valluvar builds the chapter on a pun: ஒழுக்காறு (ozhukkaaru, “the path of right conduct”) and அழுக்காறு (azhukkaaru, “the path of impurity,” i.e., envy) differ by a single sound, so the couplet sets the right road against the soiled road. He places the absence of envy inside the heart (நெஞ்சத்து), not just in outward behavior, which treats envy as a flaw of character rather than a wrong act. Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Mu. Varadarasanar read the couplet as saying freedom from envy should be held as seriously as the formal rules of ozhukkam (Chapter 14). The view is close to Aristotle's, who counted envy among the passions whose very names imply badness, and to the Buddhist idea that a disposition must be trained, not merely a deed avoided.

tamil:
விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லையார் மாட்டும்
அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Vizhuppetrin aqdhoppadhu illaiyaar maattum
Azhukkaatrin anmai perin.
current_meaning: If you can stop being jealous of anyone at all, no other good thing you could ever gain is equal to that.
elementary: Imagine a treasure chest full of prizes: gold, trophies, toys. This kural says the best prize is a heart that is never jealous of anyone. Better than all the rest.
university: The key phrase is யார் மாட்டும் (“toward anyone at all”): Valluvar asks for complete freedom from envy, not selective freedom. Envy usually targets equals, as Aristotle observed, so envying no one means refusing to compare one's own standing with others'. By calling this the highest of all விழுப்பேறு (excellent attainments), the couplet puts an inner state above wealth, fame, and learning. The point anticipates the Stoic claim that goods in our control are the only true goods, and that once we see this, “there will be no room for envy.”

tamil:
அறன்ஆக்கம் வேண்டாதான் என்பான் பிறனாக்கம்
பேணாது அழுக்கறுப் பான்.
transliteration:
Aran aakkam vendaadhaan enbaan piranaakkam
Penaadhu azhukkaruppaan.
current_meaning: Someone who is jealous when others do well, instead of being happy for them, is really saying they do not want goodness or success for themselves.
elementary: If your friend wins a prize and you sulk instead of cheering, you're not just being unkind to them. You're blocking your own chance to be good and to do well. Being jealous is like saying “I don't want good things for myself either.”
university: The couplet makes a psychological claim: envy is self-defeating, not just unkind. Parimelazhagar reads அறனாக்கம் as both அறம் (virtue) and ஆக்கம் (prosperity). The envious person's attitude implicitly rejects both, since virtue grows through goodwill and prosperity through good conduct. பேணாது (“without cherishing”) implies the right response to another's good fortune is active appreciation, close to the Buddhist mudita (sympathetic joy). Aristotle's definition fits closely: the envious man “is pained at all good fortune,” even when it is deserved.

tamil:
அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார் இழுக்காற்றின்
ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Azhukkaatrin allavai seyyaar izhukkaatrin
Edham padupaakku arindhu.
current_meaning: Wise people know the trouble that comes from doing wrong, so they will never do wrong because of jealousy.
elementary: If you know a path has a big muddy pit, you don't walk that way. Wise people know jealousy leads to doing mean things, and mean things lead to trouble, so they don't let jealousy push them into it.
university: The subject, “the wise” (அறிவுடையோர்), is understood from context, as the commentators note. The couplet treats restraint from envy-driven wrongdoing as a matter of knowledge: seeing where the “fault-path” (இழுக்காறு) leads. Valluvar moves from the feeling of envy (azhukkaaru) to the acts it produces (அல்லவை, unrighteous deeds), and the wise stop the chain at the first link. The reasoning is prudential as well as moral, like the Buddha's image of the trader who avoids a dangerous road. It also matches Aristotle's claim that envy, like theft or murder, has no right amount or right occasion; it is always a mistake.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு உடையார்க்கு அதுசாலும் ஒன்னார்
வழுக்காயும் கேடீன் பது.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaarkku adhusaalum onnaar
Vazhukkaayum kedeenbadhu.
current_meaning: For jealous people, jealousy alone is enough to ruin them. Even if their enemies fail to hurt them, their own jealousy will bring them down.
elementary: Imagine someone who never needs a bully to hurt them, because they keep hurting themselves by feeling jealous all the time. Envy is like a bully that lives inside you.
university: The phrase அது சாலும் (“that is enough”) makes envy a self-sufficient engine of destruction. No external enemy (ஒன்னார்) is needed, and even if enemies falter (வழுக்காயும்), envy does not. The same insight appears across traditions: Proverbs calls envy “the rottenness of the bones,” Ovid pictures Envy gnawing herself, and the Dhammapada compares the depraved man to a creeper that strangles its own host tree. Aristotle's definition explains why: envy is pain at another's good that brings the envier no gain, only suffering.

tamil:
கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான் சுற்றம் உடுப்பதூஉம்
உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Koduppadhu azhukkaruppaan sutram uduppadhoovum
Unbadhoovum indrik kedum.
current_meaning: A person who is jealous when others receive gifts will be ruined, and their family with them, left with no clothes to wear and no food to eat.
elementary: Imagine a kid who gets upset every time a teacher gives stickers to others. Eventually, nobody wants to share with that kid or their friends either. Being jealous of other people's gifts leaves you, and the people around you, with nothing.
university: This couplet narrows envy to a specific form: resentment of generosity itself (கொடுப்பது, “what is given”), whether one objects to a gift going to someone else or tries to stop it. The punishment is social and material: not only the envier but his சுற்றம் (kin, dependents) are left without food or clothing, since the grudging spirit cuts the household off from the web of mutual giving. The idea has a close counterpart in the Buddha's teaching that whoever obstructs another's gift harms three parties, beginning with himself. Pirkei Avot likewise names the giver who wishes others would not give as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to others.

tamil:
அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு உடையானைச் செய்யவள்
தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்.
transliteration:
Avvithu azhukkaaru udaiyaanaich cheyyaval
Thavvaiyaik kaatti vidum.
current_meaning: The goddess of good luck turns away from the jealous person and points them out to her older sister, the goddess of bad luck.
elementary: Imagine Good Luck as a friendly person who visits your house. When she sees you're always jealous, she leaves, and on her way out she tells her grumpy sister, Bad Luck, “This house is yours now.”
university: Valluvar here uses a mythological image unusual for a text that mostly avoids sectarian deities. செய்யவள் (“the red/fair one”) is Lakshmi (Tiru), and தவ்வை (“elder sister”) is Mudevi/Jyeshtha, goddess of misfortune, who in the Padma and Linga Puranas rises from the churned ocean before Lakshmi and is told to dwell among the quarrelsome and wicked. அவ்வித்து is read by Parimelazhagar as “being herself envious [of him],” so the goddess answers envy with envy, a measure-for-measure punishment. The image turns an abstract claim, that envy drives away prosperity, into a vivid scene, a technique Valluvar uses sparingly and to strong effect.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு எனஒரு பாவி திருச்செற்றுத்
தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchchetruth
Theeyuzhi uyththu vidum.
current_meaning: Jealousy is a wicked thing like no other. It wipes out a person's riches and pushes them down a path that leads to burning suffering.
elementary: Envy is like a sneaky thief who first steals everything you have, then pushes you onto a dangerous road. Once envy moves in, it takes your good things away and leads you somewhere bad.
university: Valluvar personifies envy as a பாவி (sinner, evil being) with no equal (ஒரு), and gives it two acts: it destroys wealth (திருச்செற்று, with திரு again evoking Lakshmi from the previous couplet) and drives its host into தீயுழி. The term means “evil place” or “evil path”; Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as hell, others as a life of wrongdoing. The double sense covers both this-worldly ruin and afterlife punishment, a pattern also seen in the Dhammapada's “suffers here and hereafter.” Parallels such as Korah and Devadatta, whose envy ended with the earth swallowing them, show how widely traditions have linked envy to a downward plunge.

tamil:
அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான்
கேடும் நினைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Avviya nenjathaan aakkamum sevviyaan
Kedum ninaikkap padum.
current_meaning: When a jealous person grows rich and a good, honest person falls into hard times, it is something strange that we should stop and think about.
elementary: Sometimes a mean, jealous kid seems to get everything, while a kind kid has a hard time. That looks unfair, and this kural says: stop and think about it. Things may not stay that way, and there is a deeper reason behind it.
university: Valluvar recognizes the classic problem of theodicy: the wicked sometimes prosper and the good sometimes suffer. He does not deny it. He calls these cases நினைக்கப்படும், “to be reflected upon.” Parimelazhagar resolves the anomaly through karma: the envious man's prosperity comes from past merit now being used up, and the good man's suffering from past deeds now being paid off, so neither lasts. The same wrestling appears in Psalm 73, in Rabbi Yannai's admission in Pirkei Avot, in the Dhammapada's teaching that evil “ripens” late, and in Glaucon's challenge in Plato's Republic, which makes this one of the most widely shared questions in world ethics.

tamil:
அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை அஃதுஇல்லார்
பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல்.
transliteration:
Azhukkatru akandraarum illai aqdhuillaar
Perukkaththil theerndhaarum il.
current_meaning: No one has ever become great by being jealous, and no one free of jealousy has ever lost the good things they had.
elementary: Being jealous has never helped anyone become great, not even once. And people who are happy for others never end up losing out because of it. So jealousy has zero upside, and kindness has zero downside.
university: The chapter closes with a balanced pair of universal negatives: அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை (none have grown great through envy; அகன்றார், literally “expanded”) and அஃதில்லார் பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல் (none without it have been cut off from increase). The form is a complete disjunction: envy never helps and its absence never hurts, so envy is irrational even on purely selfish grounds. Read with Kural 169, the couplet resolves the anomaly: apparent exceptions are temporary and the long-run pattern holds. The prudential argument matches Epictetus: if someone gains an advantage by paying a price you did not pay, “don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you.”

tamil:
நடுவின்றி நன்பொருள் வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றிக்
குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்.
transliteration:
Naduvindri nanporul vehkin kudiponrik
Kutramum aange tharum.
current_meaning: If you stop being fair and long to take someone else's good things, that greed will ruin your family and bring blame on you, right away.
elementary: Imagine wanting your classmate’s new bike so badly that you stop caring what is fair. This kural says that kind of wanting is like a crack in your own house: it doesn’t just get you in trouble, it hurts your whole family too.
university: The chapter opens with its thesis in its strongest form: covetousness (வெஃகுதல், vehkuthal) is condemned not only as an act of seizure but as a desire born of abandoning நடு (nadu), the equity or impartiality Valluvar had already exalted in chapter 12 (நடுவு நிலைமை). The consequences are twofold and immediate: the family line (குடி, kudi) is destroyed and guilt (குற்றம்) accrues, and the word ஆங்கே (aange, “right there, at that moment”) insists that the damage is not deferred to a future birth but arrives simultaneously with the desire. Parimelazhagar reads the kural as addressed to the householder, which explains why the penalty falls on the kudi: the covetous man betrays the very household he is supposed to sustain. The idea that injustice in acquisition corrodes the acquirer’s own house recurs across traditions, from the Hebrew story of Achan to Aristotle’s analysis of pleonexia as a vice of unfairness (anisotes).

tamil:
படுபயன் வெஃகிப் பழிப்படுவ செய்யார்
நடுவன்மை நாணு பவர்.
transliteration:
Padupayan vehkip pazhippaduva seyyaar
Naduvanmai naanu pavar.
current_meaning: People who are ashamed to be unfair will never do shameful things just because they want the profit those things could bring.
elementary: Suppose you could win a game by quietly peeking at someone’s cards. A person who would feel embarrassed to cheat just won’t do it, even if it means winning. This kural says that feeling of shame protects you from doing wrong for a prize.
university: Where kural 171 threatened consequences, 172 names the internal safeguard: நாண் (naan), a moral sense of shame or modesty, here specifically shame at நடுவன்மை (naduvanmai, “non-equity”). The phrase படுபயன் (padupayan) denotes the gain that “falls” to one, the benefit that would accrue from taking another’s property, and பழிப்படுவ (pazhippaduva) are acts that incur public blame. Valluvar’s psychology is notable: the person of integrity is restrained less by fear of punishment than by an internalised aversion to injustice, a theme developed fully in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை). This aligns with Gita ethics, in which modesty (Sanskrit hri) and the reflex of weighing gain against righteousness are marks of a mature moral agent.

tamil:
சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி அறனல்ல செய்யாரே
மற்றின்பம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Sitrinbam vehki aranalla seyyaare
Matrinbam vendu pavar.
current_meaning: People who want the other, lasting happiness will never do wrong just to grab a small pleasure that soon passes.
elementary: If you are saving your pocket money for something you really love, you won’t spend it on a cheap sweet that’s gone in a minute. This kural says people who want the big, lasting kind of happiness don’t do bad things for tiny, quick treats.
university: The kural sets up a contrast between சிற்றின்பம் (sitrinbam, “petty pleasure”) and மற்றின்பம் (matrinbam, “the other joy”). Parimelazhagar glosses the latter as the bliss of heaven or liberation, while modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan read it as the enduring happiness that flows from aram (virtue); either way, the argument is a rational trade-off, not a prohibition. Covetousness is foolish because it sacrifices a greater, lasting good for a trivial, fleeting one. This is among the most widely shared structures in world ethics: the Buddha’s ‘renounce the lesser happiness for the greater’, Nachiketas refusing Death’s riches, and Socrates rebuking Athens for preferring money to the soul all have the same shape.

tamil:
இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் புலம்வென்ற
புன்மையில் காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Ilamendru vehkuthal seyyaar pulamvendra
Punmaiyil kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People who see clearly and have control over their senses will not long for what belongs to others, even when they think, “We are poor and have nothing.”
elementary: It is easy not to want your friend’s lunch when you already have a big one. This kural is about someone who is really hungry and still doesn’t take what isn’t theirs, because they’ve trained themselves to be strong inside.
university: This kural removes the most sympathetic excuse for covetousness: need. இலம் என்று (ilam endru, “saying ‘we have nothing’”) captures the self-justifying thought of the poor, and Valluvar insists that even this does not license desire for another’s goods among those who are புலம் வென்ற (pulam venra, “sense-conquered”) and of புன்மையில் காட்சி (punmaiyil kaatchi, “vision free from meanness”). The pairing of sense-mastery with non-covetousness is characteristically Indian (compare the Gita’s sthitaprajna), but the insistence that integrity must survive poverty is universal, as Agur’s prayer in Proverbs attests. Valluvar is not romanticising poverty; he is arguing that virtue that fails under pressure was never virtue.

tamil:
அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவென்னாம் யார்மாட்டும்
வெஃகி வெறிய செயின்.
transliteration:
Ahki akandra arivennaam yaarmaattum
Vehki veriya seyin.
current_meaning: What good is a sharp and wide-ranging mind if its owner wants other people's things and acts foolishly toward anyone at all?
elementary: Imagine the smartest kid in class who uses their brains to trick friends out of their toys. Being clever doesn’t make that okay; it just makes the cleverness useless. This kural says being smart means nothing if greed makes you act foolishly.
university: The first line is a small masterpiece of sound and sense: அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு (ahki akandra arivu) describes knowledge that is at once narrowed to a fine point (ahku, ‘to become subtle/minute’) and broadened (akal, ‘to spread wide’), in other words both deep and wide. The rhetorical question ‘என்னாம்?’ (ennaam, ‘of what use?’) then cancels that learning entirely if its possessor, driven by covetousness, does வெறிய (veriya, senseless or improper deeds) toward யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, ‘anyone whatsoever’). The kural anticipates the chapter on learning (40-43) by insisting that intellect is not a moral safeguard; covetousness can hijack it. The Gita’s chain of desire, anger, delusion, and ‘loss of intelligence’ and Plato’s image of reason enslaved to money-making make the same diagnosis.

tamil:
அருள்வெஃகி ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் பொருள்வெஃகிப்
பொல்லாத சூழக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Arulvehki aatrinkan nindraan porulvehkip
Pollaadha soozhak kedum.
current_meaning: Even someone who wants to be kind and has stayed on the right path will be ruined if they start wanting others' riches and plotting evil ways to get them.
elementary: Think of a kid who has always been kind and helpful. If one day they start scheming to take someone else’s things, all that goodness can come crashing down. This kural says no one is so good that greed can’t ruin them.
university: The kural turns on a deliberate repetition: the same verb வெஃகு (vehku, ‘to desire’) is used for the noble desire for அருள் (arul, grace/compassion) and the base desire for பொருள் (porul, wealth). The same faculty of longing can be aimed upward or downward, and a person who has aimed it well can still redirect it disastrously. ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் (aatrinkan nindraan, ‘one who stood in the path’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the householder’s path by which grace is attained, and more broadly by modern commentators as the path of virtue; பொல்லாத சூழ (pollaadha soozha) stresses that plotting is itself ruinous, even before any theft. The kural is a warning against spiritual complacency, echoed in the Gita’s admission that the senses carry away even a striving sage, and in the Qur’anic portrait of the man raised by signs who ‘adhered to the earth’.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் விளைவயின்
மாண்டற் கரிதாம் பயன்.
transliteration:
Vendarka vehkiyaam aakkam vilaivayin
Maandar karithaam payan.
current_meaning: Do not wish for riches that come from wanting what belongs to others. When those riches finally bear fruit, the result is hardly ever good.
elementary: It’s like planting a seed you stole from your neighbour’s garden. It might grow, but the fruit tastes bitter because you know how you got it. This kural says wealth you got by grabbing others’ things never gives you a truly good harvest.
university: The kural uses an agricultural metaphor: வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் (vehkiyaam aakkam, ‘increase that comes through coveting’) is a crop, and விளைவயின் (vilaivayin, ‘at the time of its ripening’) its fruit is மாண்டற்கு அரிது (maandarku arithu, ‘hard to be excellent’). The argument concerns delayed consequences: ill-gotten gain may look like prosperity at first, but its maturation reveals its true nature. Some commentators (e.g., Solomon Pappaiah) read maandal as ‘goodness’ in enjoyment, while others read it as ‘glory’; either way the gain proves hollow. The theme of sweet-at-first, bitter-at-the-end fruit links this kural to the Gita’s account of rajasic happiness and to Proverbs’ ‘bread of deceit.’

tamil:
அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின் வெஃகாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கைப் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Ahkaamai selvaththirku yaadhenin vehkaamai
Vendum pirankaip porul.
current_meaning: If you ask what keeps your riches from shrinking, the answer is this: do not want the things that are in someone else's hands.
elementary: If you want to keep your own toys safe, the best rule is never to grab other people’s toys. Then no one has a reason to take yours, and you stay happy with what you have. This kural says not wanting other people’s things is the secret to keeping your own.
university: The kural is built on a pun that is lost in translation: அஃகாமை (ahkaamai, ‘non-diminishing’) and வெஃகாமை (vehkaamai, ‘non-coveting’) differ by a single consonant, so the grammar of the line enacts its claim that the one secures the other. It is framed as a riddle with its own answer (‘yaadhenin…’, ‘if one asks what…’), a didactic device Valluvar uses often. பிறன் கைப் பொருள் (piran kaip porul, ‘property in another’s hand’) pointedly includes even possessions casually within reach. The ethical logic is both moral and practical: a society in which people do not covet is one in which everyone’s wealth is secure, and a mind that does not covet does not feel its own wealth as insufficient. The kural thus unites the tenth commandment’s social function with the Upanishadic ‘do not covet’ as a spiritual discipline.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும்
திறன்அறிந் தாங்கே திரு.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu vehkaa arivudaiyaarch serum
Thiranarin thaange thiru.
current_meaning: The goddess of good fortune knows the worth of wise people who understand what is right and do not want others' things, and she finds her own way to them.
elementary: Imagine good luck as a friend who likes visiting kind, honest people. This kural says if you know what’s right and don’t try to take other people’s things, good fortune will find its way to your door by itself.
university: திரு (thiru), glossed by all traditional commentators as Lakshmi (Thirumagal), the goddess of fortune, is here personified as an agent with judgment: திறன் அறிந்து (thiran arindhu) means she ‘knows the proper way’ or ‘recognises their merit’ and arrives ஆங்கே (aange, ‘right there’). The kural thus reverses the covetous logic: the coveter reaches for wealth and loses it, while the one who does not reach is sought out by wealth itself. Parimelazhagar’s gloss emphasises that these people are அறிவுடையார் (arivudaiyaar) who know aram, so their restraint is a considered moral choice, not mere passivity. The idea that virtue attracts prosperity has close analogues in the Gita’s closing verse (where ‘sri’ accompanies righteousness), Socrates’ ‘from virtue come money and every other good’, and the Buddhist teaching that the righteous non-coveter may reappear among those of ‘great property’.

tamil:
இறலீனும் எண்ணாது வெஃகின் விறல்ஈனும்
வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Iraleenum ennaadhu vehkin viraleenum
Vendaamai ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Wanting others’ things without thinking about the result leads to ruin. The great strength of not wanting them leads to victory.
elementary: Grabbing for something that isn’t yours without thinking is like reaching into a fire: you get burned. But being strong enough to say “I don’t need that” is like winning a race. This kural says not wanting is a kind of superpower.
university: The chapter closes with a perfectly balanced antithesis built on a rhyme: இறல் ஈனும் (iral eenum, ‘gives birth to destruction’) against விறல் ஈனும் (viral eenum, ‘gives birth to victory’). The verb ஈன் (een, ‘to bear, as offspring’) makes both outcomes the natural children of their causes. எண்ணாது (ennaadhu, ‘without reflecting’) identifies thoughtlessness about consequences as the root of covetousness, while வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு (vendaamai ennum serukku) calls non-desire a kind of செருக்கு (serukku, ‘pride, exaltation, greatness’). Valluvar reclaims a word usually negative and makes it the dignity of the person who needs nothing from others. The idea that restraint is itself a victory appears in Epictetus, in the Qur’anic promise of success to those saved from their own avarice, and in the Buddhist ‘craving-freed’ who vanquishes all suffering.

tamil:
அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ஒருவன்
புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Arangooraan alla seyinum oruvan,
Purangooraan endral inidhu.
current_meaning: A person may never speak about goodness and may do only wrong. Still, it is good if people can say, “At least they do not talk badly about others behind their backs.”
elementary: Imagine a kid who forgets his homework, is messy, and gets into trouble a lot. But everyone says, “He never talks badly about anyone when they’re not around.” That one good thing still shines. This kural says not gossiping about people behind their backs is so important that even someone with lots of faults earns a little praise for it.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately provocative concession: he imagines a man who neither professes aram (virtue) nor practises it, and still finds one thing worth saying in his favour — that he is not a backbiter (puṟaṅkūṟāṉ, literally “one who speaks at the back”). The rhetorical move establishes a hierarchy of vices before any argument is made: slander is placed so low that merely abstaining from it counts as a redeeming trait. The verb “enṟal” (“that it be said”) is significant; the good in question is reputational, located in what the community can truthfully say of the man, which neatly mirrors the fact that backbiting is itself a crime against another’s reputation. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the couplet as an argument a fortiori: if non-slander redeems even the unrighteous, how much more is it required of the righteous. The chapter sits in the householder section (Illaraviyal) right after Envy and Covetousness, reflecting a sequence from inner vices to their expression in speech.

tamil:
அறனழீஇ அல்லவை செய்தலின் தீதே
புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை.
transliteration:
Aranazheei allavai seydhalin theedhe,
Puranazheeip poiththu nagai.
current_meaning: Saying bad things about someone behind their back and then giving them a fake smile to their face is worse than turning away from goodness and doing wrong.
elementary: Suppose a classmate says mean things about you when you’re gone, then comes up and grins at you like your best friend. That’s worse than someone who is just openly naughty — because the fake smile is a trick. This kural says the two-faced person is worse than the openly bad one.
university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallelism: aṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying virtue”) against puṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying [someone] at the back”), with the second judged worse (tītē). What tips the scale is the final phrase poyttu nakai, “smiling falsely” — the backbiter compounds slander with a feigned intimacy in the victim’s presence. Valluvar is thus condemning not only malicious speech but hypocrisy as a structure of relationship, a split between the face and the back that corrupts the trust on which the householder’s social world rests. The claim that this is worse than open wickedness anticipates a widely shared intuition across ethical traditions: the open enemy can be guarded against, but the smiling detractor disarms his victim first. The verse also sharpens 181: there, abstaining from slander redeemed a sinner; here, slander joined to false friendliness sinks a man below the sinner.

tamil:
புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்
அறங்கூற்றும் ஆக்கத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Purangoorip poiththuyir vaazhdhalin saadhal,
Arangootrum aakkath tharum.
current_meaning: It is better to die than to live by saying bad things behind people's backs and being fake to their faces. Dying gives the real gain that the teachings of goodness speak of.
elementary: Imagine you could stay popular only by telling mean secrets about your friends and pretending to be nice to them. This kural says it’s better to lose everything than to live that way — being a good, honest person matters more than anything you could win by gossip.
university: The couplet raises the stakes from comparison of vices to a comparison between a way of life and death itself. Puṟaṅkūṟip poyttu uyir vāḻtal — “living by backbiting and falsehood” — names a whole livelihood, the courtier’s or social climber’s art of advancing by undermining others. Against this Valluvar sets cātal, death, which paradoxically yields ākkam (prosperity, gain) of the kind that aṟam-kūṟṟu, the pronouncements of the moral treatises, recognise. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss the death as dying in poverty for having refused such conduct — a reading that turns the verse into a choice between material survival bought by slander and moral gain secured by refusing it. The structure echoes a theme found across classical ethics: that there are lives not worth living, and that moral ruin is a worse fate than death.

tamil:
கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் சொல்லற்க
முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Kannindru kannarach chollinum sollarka,
Munnindru pinnokkaach chol.
current_meaning: You may even say hard, unkind things to a person's face. But never say words behind their back without thinking about the harm those words will do.
elementary: If your friend does something wrong, it’s okay to tell them straight to their face, even if it’s hard to hear. What’s not okay is saying it to others when your friend isn’t there. Say it to their face or don’t say it at all.
university: The couplet turns on a set of spatial and visual puns. Kaṇ niṉṟu (“standing before the eyes”) is paired with kaṇ aṟa (“with the eye cut off,” i.e., without kaṇṇōṭṭam, the courteous regard that Valluvar treats as a virtue in chapter 58), while muṉ niṉṟu (“having stood in front”) contrasts with piṉ nōkkā col, which carries two senses: words that do not look to consequences, and words aimed at someone’s back. Valluvar concedes a real cost — harsh, face-to-face speech is not ideal — but ranks it clearly above secret disparagement, because direct speech leaves the target free to answer, correct, or defend himself. This makes the verse a procedural ethic of speech: criticism is legitimate in principle, but its moral character depends on the presence of the person criticised. The same structure appears in legal ideals of hearing both parties and in religious norms of private, direct rebuke.

tamil:
அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை புறஞ்சொல்லும்
புன்மையாற் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aranjollum nenjaththaan anmai puranjollum,
Punmaiyaal kaanap padum.
current_meaning: When someone talks badly about others behind their backs, that small-minded habit shows that their heart is not truly good, no matter how much they talk about goodness.
elementary: Someone might always say, “Be kind! Be fair!” But if you hear them gossiping meanly about people when those people leave, you know they don’t really mean what they say. Gossip is like a window that lets you see what’s really inside a person.
university: Here Valluvar turns backbiting into evidence. The phrase aṟañ-collum neñcattāṉ — one whose heart speaks of virtue, or, as many commentators read it, one who merely talks virtue — sets up a contrast between profession and inner reality, and puṟañ-collum puṉmai (“the meanness of speaking at the back”) becomes the diagnostic sign that exposes the gap. The verse therefore makes slander not only a wrong but a symptom: a person’s habitual talk about the absent is a more reliable index of character than his public moralising. The idea that inner character leaks out through small, unguarded habits is common to many ethical traditions, and it sharpens the chapter’s treatment of hypocrisy begun in 182. Valluvar implicitly invites the listener to read people by what they say about others when those others are not present.

tamil:
பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி யுள்ளும்
திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Piranpazhi kooruvaan thanpazhi yullum,
Thirantherindhu koorap padum.
current_meaning: A person who spreads other people's faults will have their own faults searched out, and the worst ones will be chosen and told about them.
elementary: If you tell everyone about your friend’s mistakes, soon people start looking for your mistakes too — and they’ll pick the most embarrassing ones to share. Gossip is like a boomerang: it comes back to hit you.
university: The couplet states a law of reciprocity in the economy of reputation. Piṟaṉ paḻi kūṟuvāṉ (“one who speaks another’s blame”) will find that taṉ paḻi uḷḷum (“even among his own blameworthy deeds”) the ones chosen with discernment (tiṟaṉ terintu) will be spoken of. The phrase tiṟaṉ terintu is sharp: people will not merely repeat his faults but select the most damaging, just as the backbiter selected and polished the faults of others. Valluvar therefore presents slander as self-defeating — by making fault-finding normal, the slanderer licenses the same treatment of himself. The passive kūṟappaṭum (“will be spoken”) leaves the agent unspecified, allowing both a social reading (others will retaliate) and a moral-causal one akin to karma. The idea that judgment returns in the same measure is widely shared across ethical traditions.

tamil:
பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் நகச்சொல்லி
நட்பாடல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pagachchollik kelirp pirippar nagachcholli,
Natpaadal thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: People who do not know how to make friends through warm, friendly talk will say things that split people apart, even their own close friends.
elementary: Some people know how to make friends by saying kind, fun things. Others only know how to say “Did you hear what she said about you?” — and that makes friends fight. This kural says people who can’t make friends with nice words end up breaking friendships with nasty ones.
university: The verse is built on the chiastic pair paka-c-colli (“speaking so as to split”) and naka-c-colli (“speaking so as to make [people] laugh/rejoice”). Valluvar diagnoses divisive speech as a failure of social skill as much as of morality: those who cannot tēṟṟu (be sure of, master) the art of naṭpāṭal, friendship-making through genial conversation, fall back on the easier currency of tale-bearing. The object kēḷir means kin or intimates, so the damage falls on the speaker’s own circle — Parimelazhagar notes they alienate even their friends from themselves. This connects the chapter to the book’s later treatment of friendship (naṭpu, chapters 79–83) and recalls the Buddhist category of pisuṇā vācā, speech that splits people apart. The couplet implies a positive programme: cultivate the speech that unites, and the temptation to divide loses its hold.

tamil:
துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் மரபினார்
என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Thunniyaar kutramum thootrum marabinaar,
Ennaikol ethilaar maattu.
current_meaning: If people make a habit of telling everyone the faults of those closest to them, what will they not do to strangers?
elementary: If someone spreads secrets about their own best friend, imagine what they’d say about you! This kural says: watch how people talk about their closest friends — that’s how they’ll treat everyone else.
university: The couplet argues a fortiori from intimacy. Tuṉṉiyār (“those who are close”) are the people whom affection, obligation, and self-interest should all protect; if the slanderer’s marapu (settled disposition, habit) leads him to tūṟṟu (scatter abroad, as chaff is winnowed) even their faults, then no restraint can be expected toward ētilār, those who are unconnected to him. The rhetorical question ennaikol (“what indeed?”) leaves the outcome to the listener’s imagination. Valluvar is making a practical point about trust: how a person speaks of his intimates is the best predictor of how he will treat everyone else. The verse also implies that backbiting is not an occasional lapse but a trait, marapu, which, once formed, spares no one.

tamil:
அறன்நோக்கி ஆற்றுங்கொல் வையம் புறன்நோக்கிப்
புன்சொல் உரைப்பான் பொறை.
transliteration:
Arannokki aatrungol vaiyam purannokkip,
Punsol uraippaan porai.
current_meaning: The earth still carries the person who waits until someone is gone and then says mean things about them. Is that only because the earth cares about being good?
elementary: The ground holds up everyone who walks on it — good people and mean people. This kural jokes that the Earth must be very patient and kind to keep carrying a gossip who waits for people to leave so he can say nasty things about them.
university: The couplet is one of Valluvar’s sharpest ironies. Vaiyam, the earth, is imagined as a moral agent who bears (āṟṟu) the poṟai (burden, weight) of the slanderer, and the poet wonders whether it does so only aṟaṉ nōkki — out of regard for dharma, since bearing all beings is its duty. The mirrored phrases aṟaṉ nōkki and puṟaṉ nōkki are carefully placed: the earth looks toward virtue, while the slanderer looks toward the back, watching for his victim’s absence before he speaks puṉ col, base words. The image draws on the Indian idea of the earth as the patient bearer of all beings, whose forbearance (poṟai also means patience) contrasts with the slanderer’s impatience to wound. Valluvar thus makes the slanderer a dead weight on the world, tolerated only by a patience he does not deserve.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
தீதுண்டோ மன்னும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ethilaar kutrampol thankutrang kaankirpin,
Theedhundo mannum uyirkku.
current_meaning: If people could see their own faults the way they see the faults of others, could any harm ever come to anyone?
elementary: It’s easy to notice when a friend makes a mistake, but hard to notice our own. If everyone checked their own mistakes as carefully as they check others’, there would be much less gossip — and much less trouble for everyone.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter by moving from prohibition to cure. The comparison ētilār kuṟṟampōl (“like the faults of strangers”) captures the ease and even pleasure with which we see others’ failings; if that same clear sight were turned on taṉ kuṟṟam, one’s own faults, the rhetorical question asks, would any harm (tītu) remain for mannum uyir — beings who endure, or, in some commentaries, the soul that persists? The logic is psychological: backbiting feeds on an asymmetry of attention, and self-examination removes both the motive and the moral standing for it. Mu. Karunanidhi’s gloss draws out the practical point — the habit of slander disappears and life becomes peaceful. The ending thus turns the chapter’s condemnation of the slanderer into a discipline for the reader, echoing a strikingly wide range of traditions that contrast the tiny flaw in others with the large one in oneself.

tamil:
பல்லார் முனியப் பயனில சொல்லுவான்
எல்லாரும் எள்ளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Pallaar muniyap payanila solluvaan,
Ellaarum ellap padum.
current_meaning: A person who keeps talking about useless things until many listeners are fed up will be looked down on by everyone.
elementary: Imagine someone in class who keeps talking and talking about nothing while everyone is trying to listen to the teacher. Soon nobody wants to sit next to them. This kural says that people who chatter about useless things make everyone tired of them, and then everyone stops respecting them.
university: The chapter opens with a social rather than a metaphysical sanction: the idle talker is punished by the listening community itself. The verb முனிய (muniya, “to be vexed, to loathe”) names the listeners’ reaction, and எள்ளப்படும் (ellappadum, “will be scorned”) names the outcome, so the couplet traces a causal chain from speech to irritation to contempt. The contrast of பல்லார் (“the many” who hear him) with எல்லாரும் (“everyone”) is deliberate: annoyance starts with the immediate audience but reputation spreads to the whole world. Coming straight after the chapter on backbiting (புறங்கூறாமை), the kural widens the ethics of speech from malicious words to merely empty ones, treating wasted words as a real, if quieter, wrong. Plutarch’s essay on garrulousness makes the same diagnosis, that the chatterer seeks affection and wins hatred.

tamil:
பயனில பல்லார்முன் சொல்லல் நயனில
நட்டார்கண் செய்தலிற் றீது.
transliteration:
Payanila pallaarmun sollal nayanila,
Nattaarkan seydhalir reedhu.
current_meaning: Talking about pointless things in front of many people is worse than being unkind to your own friends.
elementary: If you are rude to one friend, that hurts one person. But if you stand up in front of the whole school and waste everyone’s time with silly talk, you hurt everyone’s time at once. This kural says doing that in front of many people is even worse than being unkind to a friend.
university: The couplet works through a startling comparison. Doing நயனில (nayanila, “what is devoid of goodness/propriety”) to நட்டார் (nattaar, “friends”), which is a real ethical fault, is ranked below speaking பயனில (payanila, “what is devoid of benefit”) before பல்லார் (“the many”). The two phrases rhyme (nayanila / payanila), and the parallel sound makes the ranking stick in the ear. The argument depends on scale and publicity: an unkind act toward a friend stays in a private relationship that can be repaired, while empty talk before an assembly wastes the attention of many people at once and fixes one’s public character. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all keep this ‘worse than’ reading, which shows how seriously Valluvar takes the public squandering of speech.

tamil:
நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் பயனில
பாரித் துரைக்கும் உரை.
transliteration:
Nayanilan enbadhu sollum payanila,
Paarith thuraikkum urai.
current_meaning: When a person goes on and on about useless things, their talk itself shows everyone that they are not a good person.
elementary: You can often tell what kind of person someone is just by listening to them. If a person keeps talking on and on about useless things, their own words are like a sign on their back that says, “I am not a good person.” They don’t even need anyone else to say it.
university: The grammar is striking: the subject of சொல்லும் (“will declare”) is the talk itself (உரை, urai), so speech bears witness against the speaker. பாரித்து (paarittu, “spreading out, amplifying”) condemns not a single slip but the habit of stretching trivial matter into long discourse. The key term நயனிலன் (nayanilan, “one without nayan”) is glossed differently by modern commentators: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as lacking virtue (aram), Solomon Pappaiah as lacking justice (neethi), and Kalaignar as simply a ‘useless person’. All of these readings agree that speech works as a public index of inner character. The same idea appears in Solon’s maxim that speech is the image of actions, and in the Buddha’s teaching that discernment is revealed through conversation.

tamil:
நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும் பயன்சாராப்
பண்பில்சொல் பல்லா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Nayansaaraa nanmaiyin neekkum payansaaraap,
Panbilsol pallaa rakaththu.
current_meaning: Useless, rude words spoken in front of many people pull a person away from goodness and take away the good in them.
elementary: Think of a garden. Every time you throw rubbish into it, the flowers have less room to grow. Rude, useless talk in front of others is like throwing rubbish into your own heart’s garden. Bit by bit, it pushes the good things out.
university: The couplet is built on two paired negatives, பயன்சாரா (“not joined to benefit”) and நயன்சாரா (“not joined to nayan”, i.e., virtue or propriety), with பண்பில் (panpil, “uncultured, graceless”) in between. The claim is about moral formation, not reputation: such speech நன்மையின் நீக்கும் (“removes one from goodness”), gradually alienating the speaker from his own better character. Mu.
