Varadarasan reads the result as ‘not joining with aram and being removed from good’, while Kalaignar stresses that it also destroys the listeners’ pleasure. The setting பல்லாரகத்து (“among many”) again marks public speech as the place where habits of character are formed. The same point appears in Paul’s warning that ‘vain babblings’ ‘increase unto more ungodliness’ and in the Buddha’s listing of idle chatter among unrighteous conduct.

tamil:
சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் பயனில
நீர்மை யுடையார் சொலின்.
transliteration:
Seermai sirappodu neengum payanila,
Neermai yudaiyaar solin.
current_meaning: If even good people speak empty, useless words, they lose both their good name and the respect it earned them.
elementary: Imagine a famous, respected captain of a sports team. If she starts saying silly, pointless things all the time, the team slowly stops looking up to her. This kural says that even good people lose their respect if they fill the air with useless words.
university: This kural turns from the habitual babbler to the virtuous person who lapses. நீர்மையுடையார் (neermaiyudaiyaar) means those who have fine nature, literally a ‘watery’ or gentle disposition. The couplet warns that they are not immune: their சீர்மை (seermai, ‘excellence, eminence’) departs together with its சிறப்பு (sirappu, ‘honour, distinction’). Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘அப்பொழுதே’ (‘at that very moment’), stressing how suddenly the loss comes. The point is that reputation is a fragile social credit, and vain talk spends it faster than virtue earns it. Ecclesiastes’ image of dead flies spoiling the perfumer’s ointment is perhaps the closest cross-cultural parallel.

tamil:
பயனில்சொல் பாராட்டு வானை மகன்எனல்
மக்கட் பதடி யெனல்.
transliteration:
Payanilsol paaraattu vaanai makanenal,
Makkat padhadi yenal.
current_meaning: Do not call someone who loves to show off with empty words a real person. Call them the useless husk among people.
elementary: When farmers harvest rice, the good grain is kept and the light, empty husks called chaff blow away in the wind. This kural says a person who only talks empty talk is like that chaff: they look like a person on the outside, but inside there is nothing useful.
university: Valluvar here turns from consequence to classification. பாராட்டுவான் (paaraattuvaan) means one who displays, cherishes or keeps repeating; Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as ‘saying many times’. The one who does this with பயனில்சொல் (empty words) is denied the name மகன் (makan, ‘man, human being’) and given instead மக்கட்பதடி (makkat-padhadi, ‘the chaff of humanity’). The agricultural metaphor is precise: chaff (பதர்) has the outward form of grain without its kernel, so the babbler has the form of a person without the substance that makes speech human. (One web edition prints ‘பராட்டு’ here, evidently a typo; the standard reading ‘பாராட்டு’ is followed.) The image anticipates later critiques of inauthentic ‘idle talk’, such as Heidegger’s Gerede, in which speech circulates without anyone really grasping what it is about.

tamil:
நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக சான்றோர்
பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Nayanila sollinum solluka saandror,
Payanila sollaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Good people may say things that are not pleasant if they must. But it is good for them never to say things that are useless.
elementary: A good coach may sometimes say something that stings, like “You need to practise harder!” That isn’t nice to hear, but it helps. What a good coach should never do is waste the team’s time with pointless chatter. This kural says: a hard word that helps is okay, but a useless word is not.
university: This is the chapter’s most philosophically daring couplet, because it ranks the two standards of speech against each other. நயனில (nayanila) is glossed by Kalaignar as ‘not sweet or pleasant’, by Pappaiah as ‘unjust’ and by Mu. Varadarasan as ‘lacking aram’. On the milder reading, Valluvar concedes that the சான்றோர் (saandror, the noble or accomplished) may speak unpleasantly, but insists that they must never speak uselessly. So usefulness (பயன்) is made the non-negotiable floor of speech, and pleasantness (நயன்) is a desirable but negotiable quality. This differs from Manu’s well-known rule against ‘disagreeable truth’, and it lines up closely with the Buddha’s criteria in the Abhaya Sutta, where beneficial but unwelcome words may be spoken at the right time and unbeneficial words never.

tamil:
அரும்பயன் ஆயும் அறிவினார் சொல்லார்
பெரும்பயன் இல்லாத சொல்.
transliteration:
Arumpayan aayum arivinaar sollaar,
Perumpayan illaadha sol.
current_meaning: Wise people who look for rare and valuable benefits never say words that do not bring great benefit.
elementary: If you are hunting for gold, you don’t fill your bag with ordinary pebbles. Wise people are like gold-hunters with their words: they only say things that are really valuable, and they don’t waste words on things that don’t matter.
university: The couplet raises the standard. It is not enough for words to have some பயன் (benefit): the wise refuse words lacking பெரும்பயன் (perumpayan, ‘great benefit’). The rhyme of அரும்பயன் (arumpayan, ‘rare benefit’) with பெரும்பயன் binds the two halves together: those who investigate (ஆயும், aayum) rare and valuable ends apply the same selectiveness to their own speech. This describes an intellectual temperament as much as an ethical rule, since the discerning mind that weighs what is worth pursuing also weighs what is worth saying. The Upanishadic command to ‘leave off other words’, Shammai’s ‘speak little’ and Homer’s portrait of Menelaus as ‘a man of few words’ all praise the same economy of speech.

tamil:
பொருள்தீர்ந்த பொச்சாந்துஞ் சொல்லார் மருள்தீர்ந்த
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Poruldheerndha pochchaandhum sollaar maruldheerndha,
Maasaru kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People who see clearly, with no confusion or fault in their thinking, will not speak meaningless words, not even by mistake.
elementary: Some people are so careful and clear-headed that even when they are tired or distracted, they don’t blurt out silly things. This kural says that people whose minds are truly clean and clear don’t say empty words even by accident.
university: The couplet balances two phrases built on தீர்ந்த (theerndha, ‘ended, freed of’). The speech is பொருள்தீர்ந்த (‘emptied of meaning’), and the speakers are மருள்தீர்ந்த (‘freed of delusion’). The symmetry suggests that meaningless words can only come from a mind that still holds some confusion. பொச்சாந்தும் (pochchaandhum, ‘even through forgetfulness/heedlessness’) raises the standard from deliberate restraint to spontaneous purity: the மாசறு காட்சியவர் (maasaru kaatchiyavar, ‘those of flawless insight’) do not need to police their tongues, because nothing empty is left in them to come out. Pochchaappu (heedlessness) later gets a chapter of its own (ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை), which shows how central vigilance is to Valluvar’s ethics. There is a close parallel in the Buddhist portrait of the freed person whose ‘speech is calm’ and in James’s ‘perfect man’ who ‘offends not in word’.

tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய சொல்லற்க
சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Solluka sollir payanudaiya sollarka,
Sollir payanilaach sol.
current_meaning: Of all the words you could say, say only the useful ones. Never say the ones that are useless.
elementary: Before you speak, ask yourself one simple question: “Will this help?” If the answer is yes, say it. If the answer is no, don’t. That’s the whole rule, and this kural says it in the simplest way possible.
university: The chapter closes with one of the most famous sound-patterns in the Kural. Forms of சொல் (sol, ‘word/speak’) occur five times: சொல்லுக (‘speak’), சொல்லில் (‘among words’, twice), சொல்லற்க (‘do not speak’) and சொல் (‘word’). The only thing that changes between the positive and negative halves is பயனுடைய / பயனிலா (‘useful / useless’). The form enacts the content: a couplet made almost entirely of the word ‘word’ shows perfect economy, with nothing wasted. Solomon Pappaiah reads பயன் as the three classical aims of life (aram, porul, inbam), which ties the rule to the whole structure of the Kural. The maxim sums up the chapter as a single test that can be applied to every utterance, much like Epictetus’s ‘speak merely what is necessary’ and the hadith ‘speak good or keep quiet’.

tamil:
தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்
தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Theevinaiyaar anjaar vizhumiyaar anjuvar,
Theevinai ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Bad people are not afraid of the pride that comes from doing wrong. Truly good people are afraid of it.
elementary: Imagine two kids near a hot stove. One has touched it so many times he doesn’t even flinch anymore. The other is careful and keeps her hands away. This kural says good people are like the careful kid — they are scared of doing bad things, while people who do bad things all the time have stopped being scared at all.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a paradox: fear, usually a mark of weakness, is here the mark of excellence (விழுமியார், “the eminent”). The object of dread is not punishment but “the pride called evil-doing” (தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு) — Parimelazhagar reads செருக்கு as the intoxication or swagger that evil deeds produce, which dulls conscience the more one indulges it. The couplet thus describes moral desensitization: habitual wrongdoers lose the very faculty of dread that protects the noble. This anticipates what Buddhist ethics calls hiri-ottappa (moral shame and moral dread) and Jewish ethics calls yirat cheit (fear of sin) — fear reconceived as a moral sense rather than cowardice.

tamil:
தீயவை தீய பயத்தலால் தீயவை
தீயினும் அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyavai theeya payaththalaal theeyavai,
Theeyinum anjap padum.
current_meaning: Bad deeds lead to more bad things, so we should fear bad deeds even more than we fear fire.
elementary: Fire can burn you, so you keep away from it. But a bad deed is even worse than fire — one bad deed leads to another bad deed, and then another, like sparks starting more fires. So we should be even more careful about doing bad things than about touching fire.
university: The couplet is built on a deliberate pun: தீ means both “evil” and “fire,” and தீயவை (“evil things”) sounds like “fiery things.” Valluvar’s argument is comparative — fire burns only what it touches and can be put out, but evil propagates, generating consequences for both the victim and the doer (Pulavar Kesigan: ‘to others and to oneself’). Evil is therefore self-replicating in a way fire only resembles. The same insight — that wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing — appears in the rabbinic dictum that ‘one transgression leads to another’ and in Aeschylus’s image of the evil deed that begets its own offspring.

tamil:
அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலையென்ப தீய
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்.
transliteration:
Arivinul ellaan thalaiyenba theeya,
Seruvaarkkum seyyaa vidal.
current_meaning: Wise people say the highest wisdom of all is not doing bad things even to those who hurt us.
elementary: If someone knocks down your sandcastle, you might want to knock down theirs. But the smartest thing — smarter than anything in any book — is to not do something bad back. Being kind even to someone who was mean to you is the cleverest thing of all.
university: Here Valluvar relocates the virtue of non-retaliation from the realm of emotion (forgiveness) into the realm of intellect: it is the ‘head’ (தலை) of all knowledge. செறுவார் means those who actively hurt or oppress one — genuine enemies, not mere irritants. The claim is that true intelligence sees what the vengeful cannot: that returning evil only multiplies it (the logic of 202) and binds the retaliator to the same consequences. The idea stands in striking agreement with Socrates in the Crito, who argues on rational grounds that one must never return wrong for wrong.

tamil:
மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க சூழின்
அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு.
transliteration:
Marandhum pirankedu soozharka soozhin,
Aransoozhum soozhndhavan kedu.
current_meaning: Do not plan someone else's ruin, not even without thinking. If you do, goodness itself will plan the ruin of the one who planned it.
elementary: It’s like throwing a boomerang at someone — it comes flying back at you. This kural says even thinking up a plan to hurt someone is like that boomerang: goodness itself will turn the plan around so it lands on you.
university: The verb சூழ் (‘to plan, surround, encompass’) is repeated three times, mirroring the plot and counter-plot: the schemer ‘surrounds’ another’s ruin, and Aram (Virtue, personified by Solomon Pappaiah as அறக்கடவுள், the deity of Virtue) ‘surrounds’ the schemer’s ruin in turn. Note the extreme standard set by மறந்தும் (‘even in forgetfulness’): not merely the deed but even a passing intention to harm is forbidden. The textual tradition is worth noting — Project Madurai and thirukkural.net print அறஞ்சூழம், but the standard reading followed by commentators and kuraltheni.com is அறஞ்சூழும் (‘will plot’). The ‘plot that recoils on the plotter’ is a near-universal motif, from Haman’s gallows to Hesiod’s ‘evil planned harms the plotter most’.

tamil:
இலன்என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க செய்யின்
இலனாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Ilan endru theeyavai seyyarka seyyin,
Ilanaagum matrum peyarththu.
current_meaning: Do not do bad things because you are poor. If you do, you will only end up even poorer.
elementary: Suppose you have no snacks and you take someone else’s lunch. Now nobody trusts you, nobody shares with you, and you might get in big trouble. You end up with even less than before! Being poor is never a good reason to do bad things — it just makes things worse.
university: Valluvar anticipates the most sympathetic excuse for wrongdoing — need — and refuses it. இலன் (‘one who has not’) is echoed in the second line (இலனாகும், ‘becomes one who has not’) with பெயர்த்து (‘again, once more’), producing a circular structure that mirrors the poverty trap itself: evil committed to escape want returns one to want. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read இலன் as ‘poor’; Pulavar Kesigan offers an alternative — ‘do not harm someone because he is without support’ — which shifts the focus to exploiting the weak. On the dominant reading, the couplet makes a hard-headed point: ill-gotten means destroy trust, reputation and future prosperity, and so perpetuate the very lack they were meant to cure.

tamil:
தீப்பால தான்பிறர்கண் செய்யற்க நோய்ப்பால
தன்னை அடல்வேண்டா தான்.
transliteration:
Theeppaala thaanpirarkan seyyarka noippaala,
Thannai adalvendaa thaan.
current_meaning: If you do not want pain and trouble to hurt you, never do bad things to others.
elementary: If you don’t want anyone to pull your hair, don’t pull anyone else’s hair. This kural says: if you don’t want bad things to happen to you, don’t do bad things to other people.
university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel compounds — தீப்பால (‘things of the evil kind’) done to others, and நோய்ப்பால (‘things of the suffering kind’) that might afflict oneself — so that the grammar itself enacts reciprocity. Commentators agree the sense is causal: suffering that ‘attacks’ (அடல்) a person is the return of the evil he has done. The argument is prudential and universal — anyone who does not want pain has a reason not to inflict it — which makes this Valluvar’s version of the negative Golden Rule. That rule appears independently in the Mahabharata, in Hillel, in Isocrates, in the Buddha and in the Gospels, one of the most striking convergences in world ethics.

tamil:
எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் வினைப்பகை
வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்.
transliteration:
Enaippakai yutraarum uyvar vinaippakai,
Veeyaadhu pinsendru adum.
current_meaning: People can escape even the worst enemies. But the enemy made by their own bad deeds never goes away. It follows them and destroys them.
elementary: You can hide from a bully, run away, or make friends again. But the bad things you did are like a shadow-monster that follows you everywhere. You can’t hide from it or run away from it, because it comes from you.
university: The contrast is between பகை (enmity) from others and வினைப்பகை (‘the enmity of deeds’) — Valluvar’s striking personification of karma as a relentless personal foe. Human enemies can be escaped, appeased or outlived (உய்வர், ‘they survive’); the enemy that is one’s own past action ‘does not perish’ (வீயாது), ‘goes behind’ (பின்சென்று) and ‘kills’ (அடும்). The image of pursuit is shared with the Greek Erinyes, who hound Orestes across the world, and with the Mahabharata’s calf that unfailingly finds its mother among a thousand cows. The couplet thus answers a common hope of wrongdoers — that they might outrun consequences.

tamil:
தீயவை செய்தார் கெடுதல் நிழல்தன்னை
வீயாது அடிஉறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Theeyavai seydhaar kedudhal nizhaldhannai,
Veeyaadhu adiyuraindh thatru.
current_meaning: Ruin stays with people who do bad things, just as a person's shadow never leaves them and stays right at their feet.
elementary: Try running away from your shadow — you can’t! It sticks to your feet wherever you go. This kural says trouble sticks to people who do bad things in the same way. It follows them everywhere.
university: Valluvar sharpens the pursuit image of 207 into a simile of inseparability: the shadow does not merely follow but ‘dwells at the feet’ (அடியுறை) — the phrase also evokes a servant or dependent who lives at one’s feet. A shadow is produced by the person himself, so the image implies that ruin is not an external punishment but a by-product of one’s own action, as inseparable as it is self-generated. The text itself shows a scribal wrinkle: Project Madurai and thirukkural.net read ‘அஇஉறைந்’, an evident typographical corruption; ytamizh.com and kuruvirotti.com give அடிஉறைந் (‘dwelling at the feet’), the reading adopted here. The shadow simile famously also appears in the second verse of the Dhammapada, but applied to good deeds.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காதல னாயின் எனைத்தொன்றும்
துன்னற்க தீவினைப் பால்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaadhala naayin enaiththondrum,
Thunnarka theevinaip paal.
current_meaning: If you truly love yourself, do not go near any bad deed at all, even a small one.
elementary: If you love yourself, you take care of yourself — you brush your teeth and wear a helmet on your bike. This kural says that taking care of yourself also means staying away from bad deeds, even tiny ones, because they end up hurting you.
university: Valluvar here turns self-love (தன்னைத்தான் காதலன்) — often treated as a vice — into the very motive for virtue: anyone who genuinely wishes himself well will keep away from evil. The key intensifier is எனைத்தொன்றும் (‘any whatsoever, however slight’), and the verb துன்னற்க means ‘do not approach or come near’, implying avoidance of the whole territory of evil (தீவினைப் பால், ‘the side/portion of evil’) rather than only its grave acts. This is a form of ‘enlightened self-interest’: properly understood, self-love and morality coincide. Aristotle makes the same argument in Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, and the Dhammapada puts it in almost the same words: ‘If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.’

tamil:
அருங்கேடன் என்பது அறிக மருங்கோடித்
தீவினை செய்யான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Arungedan enbadhu arika marungodith,
Theevinai seyyaan enin.
current_meaning: Know this: a person who never steps off the right path to do wrong will be safe from ruin.
elementary: When you walk on a narrow bridge, you’re safe as long as you don’t step off the sides. This kural says life is like that bridge: if you never wander off the good path to do bad things, nothing can really ruin you.
university: The chapter closes on a note of assurance rather than warning. அருங்கேடன் combines அரு (‘rare/absent’) with கேடு (‘ruin’): ‘one for whom ruin is rare or impossible’. The pivotal image is மருங்கோடி — ‘running off to the side’ — which pictures righteousness as a straight road and evil as a swerve off it; Parimelazhagar and later commentators read it as ‘deviating from the proper path’. After nine couplets on the consequences of evil, Valluvar states the positive corollary: since ruin comes from one’s own deeds, the one who does not swerve has nothing to fear. The swerve metaphor has close parallels in Proverbs (‘turn not to the right hand nor to the left’), in the Isha Upanishad’s prayer against ‘crooked’ sin, and in Aristotle’s virtue as a mean between deviations.

tamil:
கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு மாரிமாட்டு
என்ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு.
transliteration:
Kaimmaaru vendaa kadappaadu maarimaattu
En aatrung kollo ulagu.
current_meaning: Real helping does not expect anything back. What does the world ever give back to the rain cloud that waters it?
elementary: The rain falls on everyone's fields and never sends a bill. Nobody pays the clouds back, and the clouds never ask. This kural says good people help others the same way — just because it is right, not to get something back.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by naming the virtue kadappaadu — literally ‘what is owed, what cannot be set aside’ — and then startles the reader by saying this obligation expects no repayment. The rhetorical question (en aatrum kollo, ‘what does it do?’) is read by Parimelazhagar as an emphatic ‘nothing at all’: living beings return nothing to the clouds, so those who resemble clouds do not calculate returns either. Manakkudavar glosses kadappaadu directly as oppuravu, defining it as giving suited to one's means to the deserving without seeking recompense. The image deliberately recalls Chapter 2 (Vaan Sirappu, the Excellence of Rain), turning a cosmological fact into an ethical model: the benefactor is a natural force of sustenance, not a party to a contract. The paradox — a duty that is binding yet unrepaid — anticipates later debates about whether generosity can be obligatory without becoming exchange.

tamil:
தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு
வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Thaalaatrith thandha porulellaam thakkaarkku
Velaanmai seydhar poruttu.
current_meaning: All the money a person earns through hard work is meant for one thing: helping people who deserve help.
elementary: Imagine you worked all summer and saved up money. This kural says the best reason to work hard and earn is so that you have something to share with people who really need it.
university: The first line honours effort (thaal aatri, ‘exerting one's foot/strength’), so the kural is not a critique of wealth but a statement of its telos. Velaanmai here does not mean agriculture but ubakaram, beneficence — Parimelazhagar glosses it as oppuravu seydhal, adding that wealth is not meant for eating alone or for hoarding until it is lost. Thakkaar, ‘the worthy,’ introduces discernment: Manakkudavar defines oppuravu as giving to fitting recipients in proportion to one's income, which distinguishes it from the indiscriminate almsgiving of the next chapter (Eekai). The couplet thus rejects both the miser and the ascetic view of wealth, proposing instead a stewardship model in which earnings are held in trust for the community.

tamil:
புத்தே ளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும் பெறலரிதே
ஒப்புரவின் நல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Puththe lulagaththum eendum peralaridhe
Oppuravin nalla pira.
current_meaning: Neither in the world of the gods nor here on earth is it easy to find anything as good as helping others.
elementary: If you searched every place — here and even up in heaven — for the very best thing a person can do, you would find nothing better than helping others. It is the top prize of all good deeds.
university: Parimelazhagar gives an ingenious reason for why oppuravu is rare even in heaven: in the world of the gods all are equal, so there are neither givers nor receivers and the virtue cannot be practised; on earth nothing else benefits everyone so equally. He also records a variant reading, peRaRkaridhu, which some commentators took to mean ‘the means to obtain it is rare.’ With 211 and 212, he notes, this couplet completes the chapter's praise of oppuravu before Valluvar turns to its practice. The comparison of heaven and earth is a recurring Tamil device (cf. Kural 23) for asserting a value's absolute primacy, here placing social beneficence above ritual or ascetic merit.

tamil:
ஒத்த தறிவான் உயிர்வாழ்வான் மற்றையான்
செத்தாருள் வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Oththa tharivaan uyirvaazhvaan matraiyaan
Seththaarul vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: Only a person who knows how to help others in the right way is truly alive. Anyone else, though still breathing, counts as dead.
elementary: A person who never helps anyone is like a statue — they are there, but they do not really take part in life. This kural says being truly alive means knowing how to help the people around you.
university: The text reproduced here follows the reading ஒத்த தறிவான் (oththadhu arivaan, ‘one who knows what is fitting’) given with Parimelazhagar's commentary; some modern editions print ஒத்த தறவோன் (‘one of fitting virtue’), a variant worth noting. Parimelazhagar glosses oththadhu as ulaga nadai, ‘the conduct of the world,’ and explains that a person who lacks its knowledge and practice shows no sign of the soul's intelligence and action, and so is reckoned dead. He adds a striking remark: a lapse in worldly conduct, unlike a lapse in Vedic rite, has no expiation. The kural thus defines life socially rather than biologically — a theme with parallels from Aristotle's political animal to rabbinic sayings about the ‘living dead.’

tamil:
ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந் தற்றே உலகவாம்
பேரறி வாளன் திரு.
transliteration:
Ooruni neernirain thatre ulagavaam
Perari vaalan thiru.
current_meaning: The riches of a wise person who loves to help the world are like a village pond filled to the top, there for everyone to use.
elementary: Think of a big water tank in the middle of a village that everyone fills their pots from. When a wise, kind person becomes rich, their money is like that full tank: the whole village benefits.
university: Ooruni is specifically the common tank from which a village draws its drinking water, a piece of shared infrastructure in Tamil rural life. Parimelazhagar notes the figure of speech — ‘filling’ really belongs to the water but is attributed to the tank — and explains the point: such wealth does not go to waste but lasts long and unfailingly supplies everyone's needs. Ulagu avaam (‘desiring the world’) is read by Parimelazhagar as loving and practising ulaga nadai, while Manakkudavar reads it as ‘desired by the whole world.’ The kural begins a triad (215-217) of public-good images — tank, fruit tree, medicinal tree — that together treat private wealth in virtuous hands as a quasi-public resource.

tamil:
பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
நயனுடை யான்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Payanmaram ulloorp pazhuththatraal selvam
Nayanudai yaankan padin.
current_meaning: When riches come to a kind, generous person, it is like a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit.
elementary: A fruit tree deep in a forest helps almost no one, but a mango tree in the middle of town feeds everyone who walks by. A kind person's money is like that town tree.
university: The emphasis falls on ul-oor, ‘inside the village’: the same fruit tree in a distant forest would be of little use, so location stands for accessibility. Parimelazhagar explains nayan (courtesy, kindly propriety) as oppuravu itself, ‘since among the many forms of worldly justice oppuravu is pre-eminent,’ and says the point is that such wealth yields benefit easily to all. Manakkudavar reads nayanudaiyaan as ‘one who is loved by others’ and adds that such wealth benefits even those who dislike him. The couplet moves beyond the tank of 215 to an image of organic, seasonal abundance, suggesting that generosity in the right person is as natural as ripening.

tamil:
மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
பெருந்தகை யான்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Marundhaagith thappaa maraththatraal selvam
Perundhagai yaankan padin.
current_meaning: When riches belong to a truly good person, they are like a healing tree that always works, with every part of it used as medicine for others.
elementary: Some trees, like the neem tree, can be used as medicine — the leaves, the bark, even the roots. A great-hearted person's money is like that tree: every part of it helps someone feel better.
university: Parimelazhagar spells out what thappaa (‘not failing’) excludes: a tree fails if it grows where it is hard to reach, if it is hidden, if it bears only in some seasons, or if it is useless — so the ideal benefactor is accessible, open, reliable, and helpful in every part. He adds that such a person relieves everyone's distress without regard to his own lack. Manakkudavar glosses thapputhal as ‘hiding’: the medicinal tree does not conceal itself from those who seek it. With this third image Parimelazhagar closes the triad on how the benefactor's wealth is used, escalating from water (sustenance) to fruit (nourishment) to medicine (healing).

tamil:
இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்
கடனறி காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Idanil paruvaththum oppuravirku olkaar
Kadanari kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People who clearly understand their duty do not stop helping others, even when they themselves have less than before.
elementary: Even when you have only one cookie left, you can still break it in half for a friend. This kural says people who truly understand duty keep helping, even when they do not have much.
university: Idan il paruvam, literally ‘a season without room,’ refers to a time when wealth has contracted; Parimelazhagar glosses it as selvam surungiya kaalam. Kadan ari kaatchi — ‘the vision that knows what is owed’ — is described by him as natural discernment of what one ought to do, so that even when everything else is given up, this is not. Manakkudavar makes the practical point that oppuravu must be done even when wealth is not abundant. Together with 219, this couplet (Parimelazhagar notes) argues that poverty is no reason to abandon oppuravu, moving the virtue from a function of surplus to a function of character.

tamil:
நயனுடையான் நல்கூர்ந்தா னாதல் செயும்நீர
செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு.
transliteration:
Nayanudaiyaan nalkoorndhaa naadhal seyumneera
Seyyaadhu amaigalaa vaaru.
current_meaning: For a kind person, being poor means only one thing: the pain of not being able to do the good things they always do.
elementary: Imagine a kid who loves sharing snacks with everyone. If one day there are no snacks to share, the kid feels sad — not because they are hungry, but because they cannot give. That sadness is what ‘being poor’ means to a kind person.
university: Valluvar redefines poverty (nalkooral) from the benefactor's point of view: it is not the loss of personal comforts but the anguish of being unable to perform the benefactions that are his nature (seyum neera). Parimelazhagar underlines this: poverty for such a person is ‘not the inability to enjoy what he would enjoy.’ The verb amaigalaa (‘cannot rest content’) captures a moral restlessness, turning the absence of means into a spiritual rather than material deprivation. Paired with 218, the couplet completes Parimelazhagar's point that oppuravu is not to be abandoned because of want.

tamil:
ஒப்புரவி னால்வரும் கேடெனின் அஃதொருவன்
விற்றுக்கோள் தக்க துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Oppuravi naalvarum kedenin aqdhoruvan
Vitrukkol thakka thudaiththu.
current_meaning: If helping others leads to ruin, that ruin is worth having, even if you had to sell yourself to get it.
elementary: Some people say, ‘If you keep giving, you will end up with nothing!’ This kural answers: even if that happens, it is worth it — being someone who helps is worth more than anything you could lose.
university: The closing couplet answers a prudential objection: oppuravu may lead to kedu, material loss. Valluvar's reply is deliberately extreme — such loss is worth acquiring by selling oneself — and Parimelazhagar notes the logic: nothing is normally bought by selling oneself, so this loss is valued above everything, because it yields lasting renown; hence ‘ruin through oppuravu is not ruin.’ Manakkudavar reframes it as a trade in which one thing is sold to buy a greater, so the apparent loss should be counted as gain. The hyperbole caps the chapter's argument: from rain (211) through wealth (212-217) and poverty (218-219) to self-sacrifice (220), oppuravu is presented as a value that no calculation of self-interest can outweigh.

tamil:
வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகைமற் றெல்லாம்
குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீர துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Variyaarkku ondru eevadhe eekai matru ellaam
Kuriyedhirppai neeradhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: Only giving to people who have nothing is true giving. Every other gift is like a trade that expects something back.
elementary: If you give your friend a sticker because you hope they will give you one back, that is really a trade. But if you give your lunch to a kid who has no lunch at all and can never pay you back, that is real giving. This kural says only the second kind counts as true giving.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition by exclusion: ஈகை (eekai) is giving to the வறியார் (the destitute), and everything else is குறியெதிர்ப்பை — a gift made with a ‘measured return’ in view, which the old commentators read as something close to a loan or a reciprocal obligation. The move sharply separates philanthropy from the neighbouring virtue of ஒப்புரவு (social beneficence, Chapter 22) and from ordinary gift exchange, which anthropologists since Marcel Mauss have shown to be governed by expectations of return. The criterion is not the size of the gift but the incapacity of the recipient to repay; that incapacity is what guarantees the purity of the motive. The same test appears in Jesus’ advice to invite those who ‘cannot recompense thee’ and in the Gita’s definition of sattvic gifts given ‘without expectation of return’, making this one of the most widely shared ethical intuitions across traditions.

tamil:
நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல்தீது மேலுலகம்
இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று.
transliteration:
Nallaaru eninum kolal theedhu melulagam
Illeninum eedhale nandru.
current_meaning: Even if someone says taking from others is a good way, taking is still bad. And even if giving did not get you into heaven, giving would still be good.
elementary: Imagine someone says, “It’s fine to always ask for other people’s snacks.” It still isn’t a good habit. And imagine someone says, “Sharing won’t win you any prize.” Sharing is still the right thing to do. Giving is good even if nobody rewards you for it.
university: The couplet is built on two concessive clauses (எனினும், ‘even if’) that strip away the usual religious sanctions: receiving is wrong even if called a நல்லாறு (good path), and giving is right even if there is no மேலுலகம் (heaven above). Parimelazhagar reads the first line as rejecting the idea that accepting alms could be meritorious, which touches a live debate in Indian thought where receiving gifts was a recognised livelihood for some groups. The second line is philosophically bolder: it makes the value of giving independent of any afterlife reward, anticipating the distinction between acting from duty and acting from hope of reward. Valluvar thus grounds generosity in its intrinsic goodness rather than in cosmic bookkeeping.

tamil:
இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல்
குலனுடையான் கண்ணே யுள.
transliteration:
Ilan ennum evvam uraiyaamai eedhal
Kulanudaiyaan kanne ula.
current_meaning: Not saying the sad words “I have nothing,” and giving anyway, is found only in a person of truly good family and character.
elementary: When someone asks for help, it is easy to say, “Sorry, I don’t have anything.” A truly good person doesn’t hide behind that excuse. Even when they have only a little, they find something to share.
university: The couplet turns on the phrase இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், ‘the misery of saying “I have not”’. Commentators divide on whose words these are: Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read it as giving before the needy person has to humiliate himself by declaring his poverty, while others (e.g. Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as the giver not pleading poverty himself even when he is in straitened circumstances. Both readings put the burden of dignity on the giver: generosity is shown most clearly when one’s means are small or the asker’s shame can be spared. குலன் (kulan), usually glossed ‘noble birth’, is best understood as nobility of character and upbringing, in line with the Kural’s repeated view that conduct, not birth, defines a person (cf. Kural 972).

tamil:
இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல் இரந்தவர்
இன்முகங் காணும் அளவு.
transliteration:
Innaadhu irakkap padudhal irandhavar
Inmugam kaanum alavu.
current_meaning: Being asked for help is painful for a giving person, but only until they see the face of the one who asked light up with joy.
elementary: When a friend is sad and asks for help, you feel a little sad too. But when you help them and they smile, your sadness melts away. This kural says the giver’s pain lasts only until they see that smile.
university: The verb இரக்கப்படுதல், ‘to be begged of’, frames the scene from the giver’s side: Parimelazhagar explains that the sight of a suppliant’s distress is itself painful to a compassionate person. That pain ends at a precise moment — அளவு, ‘up to the point’ — when the giver sees the இன்முகம், the pleasant face, of the one who has been helped. The couplet therefore locates the reward of giving in shared emotion rather than in merit, reputation or return. It also implies a standard for how to give: the gift must be large and gracious enough to change the receiver’s face, which links it with teachings such as Maimonides’ rule that charity must be given with a pleasant countenance.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பசிஆற்றல் அப்பசியை
மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral pasi aatral appasiyai
Maatruvaar aatralin pin.
current_meaning: People who train themselves by going hungry are strong. But they are less strong than people who take away the hunger of others.
elementary: Going without food on purpose takes a lot of strength. But this kural says there is an even greater strength: giving food to someone who is hungry. Helping others beats showing how tough you are.
university: The couplet plays on the word ஆற்றல் (power, strength) and the verb ஆற்று (to endure, to perform): the ascetics’ power is பசி ஆற்றல், the power to endure hunger, whereas the philanthropist’s power is to மாற்று (change, remove) hunger. Valluvar deliberately ranks the householder’s charity above the ascetic’s self-mortification — a notable claim in a culture that deeply honoured tapas, and consistent with the Kural’s high regard for the householder (Chapter 5). The same contrast between self-denial and feeding the hungry is made by Isaiah, who says the fast God wants is to ‘deal thy bread to the hungry’. The couplet effectively redefines spiritual strength in social terms.

tamil:
அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல் அஃதொருவன்
பெற்றான் பொருள்வைப் புழி.
transliteration:
Atraar azhipasi theerththal agdhoruvan
Petraan porul vaippuzhi.
current_meaning: Feeding the poor whose hunger is crushing them is the best place for a person with money to store it.
elementary: People keep money in a piggy bank or a bank to keep it safe. This kural says the safest place to keep your money is in a hungry person’s full stomach. When you feed someone, your wealth becomes goodness that can never be stolen.
university: The couplet takes the image of a treasury (பொருள் வைப்புழி, ‘the place where wealth is deposited’) and relocates it: the proper strongroom for wealth is the relief of அழிபசி, ‘destroying hunger’, suffered by those who have nothing (அற்றார்). The metaphor inverts ordinary prudence, which stores wealth by withholding it, and claims that wealth is truly secured only by giving it away. Commentators read this both as moral merit that follows the giver into future lives and as social security in this life. The same ‘treasury’ inversion appears in Jesus’ ‘treasures in heaven’, in King Munbaz’s reply in the Talmud and in the Buddhist ‘well-stored fund’ of Khp 8, showing a widely shared intuition that generosity is the only wealth immune to loss.

tamil:
பாத்தூண் மரீஇ யவனைப் பசியென்னும்
தீப்பிணி தீண்டல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Paaththoon mareeiyavanaip pasiyennum
Theeppini theendal aridhu.
current_meaning: The burning sickness called hunger will hardly ever touch someone who makes a habit of sharing their food.
elementary: Imagine a kid who always shares their snacks at school. When that kid forgets their lunch one day, everyone is happy to share with them. People who share food are rarely left hungry.
university: பாத்தூண் (pāththūṇ) means ‘divided food’, food portioned out and shared, and மரீஇ indicates something practised until it is second nature. Hunger is called தீப்பிணி, a ‘fiery disease’ or ‘evil illness’, strengthening the medical image in which sharing works as a kind of immunity. The claim can be read at three levels: morally, as merit protecting the giver; socially, as a web of reciprocity in which those who share are shared with; and economically, as the observation that shared resources are used more efficiently. The Dhammapada’s ‘Hunger is the worst disease’ and the hadith that ‘food for two is sufficient for three’ show how widespread both the disease image and the sufficiency claim are.

tamil:
ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் அறியார்கொல் தாமுடைமை
வைத்திழக்கும் வன்க ணவர்.
transliteration:
Eeththuvakkum inbam ariyaarkol thaamudaimai
Vaiththizhakkum vankanavar.
current_meaning: People with hard hearts keep their things to themselves, only to lose them in the end. Do they not know the joy of giving and of being glad about it?
elementary: Imagine a kid who hides all his toys in a box so nobody else can play with them. The toys get old, break, or get lost, and he never had fun sharing them. This kural asks: doesn’t he know how happy it feels to give?
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question (அறியார்கொல், ‘do they not know?’) directed at the வன்கணவர், literally ‘the hard-eyed’, a Tamil idiom for the pitiless and miserly. Its irony lies in the verb pair வைத்து இழக்கும், ‘keep and lose’: the miser keeps wealth in order not to lose it, yet loses it anyway, through death, theft or decay, having missed the one pleasure it could have given. ஈத்து உவக்கும் இன்பம், ‘the joy of giving and delighting’, is presented as a real and distinct pleasure available only to the giver. The argument is almost psychological rather than moral: miserliness is not only wrong but self-defeating.

tamil:
இரத்தலின் இன்னாது மன்ற நிரப்பிய
தாமே தமியர் உணல்.
transliteration:
Iraththalin innaadhu mandra nirappiya
Thaame thamiyar unal.
current_meaning: Eating alone, without sharing, just to keep your shelves full is surely worse than begging.
elementary: Begging for food feels bad. But this kural says something feels even worse: sitting alone with a big pile of food and never sharing any of it. Being lonely and greedy is sadder than being poor.
university: The comparison is deliberately shocking. In Chapter 106 (இரவு) and elsewhere, begging is treated as the lowest and most painful condition, yet here Valluvar says solitary eating is more இன்னாது (painful, wretched) than begging, and seals it with மன்ற, ‘certainly’. நிரப்பிய is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in order to fill up’ one’s wealth, so the target is not eating as such but the miser who refuses to share lest his stores shrink. தமியர் உணல் (eating alone) stands for a whole social failure; the Rig Veda makes the same point when it says the man who eats without a companion is ‘all guilt’, and Epicurus says a meal without a friend is the life of a lion or wolf.

tamil:
சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை இனிததூஉம்
ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Saadhalin innaadhadhu illai inidhadhooum
Eedhal iyaiyaak kadai.
current_meaning: Nothing is more painful than dying. But even dying feels sweet when a person can no longer give to others.
elementary: Everyone thinks the worst thing in the world is dying. But this kural says a truly kind person would feel even worse if they could never help anyone again. For them, being unable to give is the saddest thing of all.
university: The final couplet of the chapter uses a hyperbolic reversal: death, the ultimate இன்னாதது (painful thing), becomes இனிது (sweet) — the emphatic அதூஉம், ‘even that’ — at the point where giving is no longer possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). The claim measures the worth of a life by its capacity to give: a life without that capacity is, for the generous person, worse than no life. Commentators read it as describing either the giver who has lost his means or one who faces a suppliant with nothing left to offer. The closing hyperbole makes giving not merely a virtue among others but the very thing that makes life worth living, bringing the chapter to a climax.

tamil:
ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல் அதுவல்லது
ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Eedhal isaipada vaazhdhal adhuvalladhu
Oodhiyam illai uyirkku.
current_meaning: Give to people in need, and live so that people speak well of you. There is no other real gain a person can get from life.
elementary: Imagine a piggy bank you can’t take with you when you leave. The only things you really keep from life are what you gave away and the kind words people say about you because of it. Giving, and being remembered well for it, is the real prize of being alive.
university: The chapter on Renown opens by fusing it with the preceding chapter on Giving (ஈகை): ஈதல் (giving) and இசைபட வாழ்தல் (living so that isai, praise, arises) are presented as one achievement, gathered by the demonstrative அது (‘that’). The pivotal word is ஊதியம் (wages, income, profit), a commercial term deliberately applied to the உயிர் (the living soul): life is framed as a venture whose only true yield is renown generated by generosity. Classical commentary (Parimelazhagan, echoed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah) specifies giving to the poor, which anchors புகழ் in ethical action rather than mere celebrity. The couplet thus redefines ‘gain’: wealth hoarded is not profit; wealth converted into others’ welfare, and the esteem that follows, is. The same link between liberality and lasting worth appears in the Vedic hymn to Liberality and in Aristotle’s remark that the liberal are loved precisely because they give.

tamil:
உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை எல்லாம் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று
ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்.
transliteration:
Uraippaar uraippavai ellaam irappaarkku ondru
Eevaarmel nirkum pukazh.
current_meaning: All the praise that people speak comes to rest on those who give something to people who ask for help.
elementary: When grown-ups tell stories about great people, the ones everyone loves to talk about are usually the helpers, the ones who shared. Kindness is what people remember and keep talking about.
university: உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை, ‘what those who speak speak’, is read by Parimelazhagan as the praise uttered by poets and eulogists; the couplet claims that all of it ultimately ‘stands upon’ (மேல் நிற்கும்) givers. Renown is thus a social fact: it lives in the mouths of others and is conferred, not seized. The verb நிற்கும் (‘stands, abides’) implies durability; the praise settles and remains. Classical Tamil culture institutionalised exactly this in the bardic economy of Sangam patronage, where poets immortalised generous chieftains such as Pari in verse. The couplet therefore doubles as a sociology of reputation: fame follows the flow of gifts, a pattern echoed in the Buddha’s list of the visible fruits of generosity and in the Psalmist’s praise of the one who ‘hath given to the poor’.

tamil:
ஒன்றா உலகத்து உயர்ந்த புகழல்லால்
பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன் றில்.
transliteration:
Ondraa ulagaththu uyarndha pukazhallaal
Pondraadhu nirpadhu ondril.
current_meaning: In this world, nothing lasts forever except a great good name, which has no equal.
elementary: Toys break, houses get old, and even mountains slowly wear down. But a story about someone who was truly good can be told again and again for a thousand years. Good fame is the one thing that doesn’t wear out.
university: The syntax hinges on ஒன்றா, which commentators read two ways: as qualifying புகழ் (‘peerless, matchless renown’) or as describing உலகு (‘this world, where nothing stays constant’). Either way, the couplet sets renown against the Indian commonplace of impermanence (நிலையாமை), which Valluvar treats in its own chapter (34): bodies, riches and kingdoms are பொன்றும் (perishable), but உயர்ந்த புகழ், exalted renown, alone stands. This is Valluvar’s this-worldly answer to the question of immortality: not the soul’s survival, but the survival of a good name in human memory. The claim parallels the Greek heroic ideal of kleos aphthiton (‘imperishable fame’), though Valluvar grounds renown in giving rather than martial glory. Philosophers such as the Stoics would dispute it, counting reputation among things outside our control and therefore not a true good.

tamil:
நிலவரை நீள்புகழ் ஆற்றின் புலவரைப்
போற்றாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
transliteration:
Nilavarai neelpukazh aatrin pulavaraip
Potraadhu puththel ulagu.
current_meaning: If someone earns a good name that spreads across the earth and lasts, the world of the gods will honor that person even more than its own wise beings.
elementary: Imagine a class in the sky where the angels usually cheer for their own star students. But if someone down on earth does something so good that the whole world talks about it for ages, even the sky-class stops and cheers for that person instead.
university: The couplet is deliberately audacious: earthly renown outranks celestial status. Its key term is contested. புலவர் ordinarily means ‘learned ones’ or ‘poets’, but Parimelazhagan glosses it here as the devas, so that the heavenly world (புத்தேள் உலகு) ‘does not praise’ its own gods but the person whose fame fills the earth (நிலவரை, ‘to the bounds of the land’); Mu. Varadarasan follows this, and Pope renders it as heaven ceasing to laud the sage. Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read புலவர் as scholars or learned men. On any reading, Valluvar inverts the usual hierarchy in which heaven confers worth on earth: here the earth’s verdict, expressed as lasting renown, is what heaven itself acknowledges. A striking parallel is the Mahabharata story of King Indradyumna, who fell from heaven when his earthly reputation faded and regained it once living memory of his generosity was found.

tamil:
நத்தம்போல் கேடும் உளதாகும் சாக்காடும்
வித்தகர்க் கல்லால் அரிது.
transliteration:
Naththampol kedum uladhaakum saakkaadum
Viththakarkku allaal aridhu.
current_meaning: A loss that is really a gain, and a death that lets you live on in people's memory, are hard for anyone except the truly wise to achieve.
elementary: A candle gets smaller as it burns, but it lights up the whole room. Some very wise people are like that. When they give away their time, money, or even their life for others, they seem to lose, but their goodness grows and people remember them forever.
university: This is the chapter’s most paradoxical and textually difficult couplet. நத்தம் is glossed by Parimelazhagan as ஆக்கம் (increase), giving ‘a ruin that is like gain’: the loss suffered by the physical body (poverty through giving, hardship) that enlarges the ‘body of fame’ (புகழுடம்பு). சாக்காடும் உளதாகும், ‘death that becomes existence’, refers to dying in such a way that one’s renown is fixed for ever. Only the வித்தகர் (the skilled, the wise) manage this conversion of loss into gain. Commentators including Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah explain it through the Tamil idea of two bodies, the perishing body of flesh and the enduring body of renown. Cross-culturally it matches the logic of heroic or sacrificial death: Achilles’ choice at Troy, Diotima’s account of those who die ‘for the sake of leaving behind them a name’, and the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.

tamil:
தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக அஃதிலார்
தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Thondrin pukazhodu thondruka aqdhilaar
Thondralin thondraamai nandru.
current_meaning: If you are born into the world, be born with the qualities that earn a good name. If you do not have them, it would be better not to be born.
elementary: If you’re going to step onto the stage in the school play, practise hard and do your best. Showing up and doing nothing good can be worse than not showing up at all. Whatever you take part in, do it in a way people can be proud of.
university: The verb தோன்று (‘to appear, arise, be born’) occurs five times, giving the couplet an incantatory force. Two readings exist. Parimelazhagan and Pope take it as ‘being born’: if one is born, one should be born with qualities that bring renown, and for those without them it were better not to be born (Pope: ‘’twere better hide your face’). Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi read it as ‘appearing in a field’: whatever role or arena one enters, one should enter it with distinction, or not at all. The first reading is existential, the second vocational; both insist that visibility without merit is a net negative. The thought has sharp parallels: Jesus’ ‘good for that man if he had not been born’, Qoheleth’s preference for an untimely birth over a life empty of good, and the Mahabharata heroine Vidula’s maxim that it is ‘better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever’.

tamil:
புகழ்பட வாழாதார் தந்நோவார் தம்மை
இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்.
transliteration:
Pukazhpada vaazhaadhaar thannovaar thammai
Ikazhvaarai novadhu evan?
current_meaning: People who do not live in a way that earns a good name should be upset with themselves. Why are they upset with the people who look down on them?
elementary: If you didn’t study and got a bad grade, being angry at the teacher doesn’t help. It’s better to look at what you could do differently. The same goes for what people think of you: if they don’t think well of you, first check your own actions.
university: Valluvar turns from praising renown to diagnosing a common evasion: blaming one’s critics instead of oneself. The couplet sets தந்நோவார் (‘they do not grieve over themselves’) against இகழ்வாரை நோவது (‘resenting those who scorn them’) and ends in the rhetorical எவன், ‘why?’. The ethical claim is that reputation, though it lives in others’ mouths (Kural 232), is earned by one’s own conduct, so responsibility lies within. Commentators from Parimelazhagan to Karunanidhi read it as a call to self-correction rather than to resentment. The insight is widely shared: Jesus’ mote and beam, Lamentations’ question why a living man should complain of the punishment of his own sins, Zeus’s complaint in the Odyssey that mortals blame the gods for their own folly, and Epictetus’ portrait of the uninstructed person who lays the fault of his condition on others.

tamil:
வசையென்ப வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் இசையென்னும்
எச்சம் பெறாஅ விடின்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyenba vaiyaththaarkku ellaam isaiyennum
Echcham peraaa vidin.
current_meaning: Wise people say that for anyone on earth, it is a shame not to leave behind a good name.
elementary: A good camper leaves the campsite better than they found it, maybe with a helpful sign for the next visitors. Life is similar: it’s a shame to leave without leaving behind something good that people remember you by.
university: The pivotal word is எச்சம்: ‘remainder, residue, what is left over’, and by extension ‘offspring’ or ‘legacy’. Renown (இசை) is defined as the proper residue of a life; to fail to obtain it (பெறாஅ, with the poetic vowel-lengthening called அளபெடை) is வசை, reproach, and the plural subject வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் makes the standard universal. Pope captured the offspring sense: ‘Fame is virtue’s child, they say; if, then, / You childless live, you live the scorn of men.’ The idea that a person’s true progeny is their good name has a remarkable parallel in Isaiah 56:5, where the childless are promised ‘a name better than of sons and of daughters’, and in Diotima’s speech in Plato’s Symposium, where the ‘children’ of Homer and Lycurgus are their works. The Islamic teaching on what continues after death (ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, a righteous child) offers a devotional analogue: what a person leaves behind continues to count.

tamil:
வசையிலா வண்பயன் குன்றும் இசையிலா
யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyilaa vanpayan kundrum isaiyilaa
Yaakkai poruththa nilam.
current_meaning: When the land carries the body of a person with no good name, its rich, healthy harvest will grow smaller.
elementary: Think of a garden where one plant takes all the water and sunshine but never gives flowers or fruit. The whole garden does a little worse because of it. A person who takes from the world but gives nothing good back is a bit like that plant.
university: Here Valluvar moves from social reproach to cosmic consequence: the earth (நிலம்) that ‘bears’ (பொறுத்த) a renownless body (இசையிலா யாக்கை) suffers a decline (குன்றும்) in its bountiful, faultless yield (வசையிலா வண்பயன்). The choice of யாக்கை, the bare physical frame, pointedly denies such a person any fuller identity: they are mere body, a burden on the ground. The underlying belief, common to many ancient cultures, links moral quality to fertility: righteous people and rulers bring rain and harvest, the unrighteous bring dearth, an idea found in the Gita’s cycle of rain and sacrifice, the Buddha’s discourse on unprincipled kings, and Homer’s blameless king under whom the earth yields abundantly. Modern readers may take it as a vivid image of free-riding: a life that consumes without contributing diminishes the common stock, close to Cicero’s charge that the self-absorbed are ‘traitors to social life’.

tamil:
வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் இசையொழிய
வாழ்வாரே வாழா தவர்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyozhiya vaazhvaare vaazhvaar isaiyozhiya
Vaazhvaare vaazhaa thavar.
current_meaning: People who live without blame are the ones who truly live. People who live without a good name are not really living at all.
elementary: Being alive is like being given a notebook. Some people fill it with kind, brave, helpful stories. Others leave it empty or scribble unkind things. Valluvar says only the first kind are really ‘living’; the others just have the notebook.
university: The chapter closes with a chiastic couplet built on repetition: வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் / இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழாதவர். The halves pivot on a near-rhyme, வசை (blame) and இசை (renown), so that ‘living without blame’ and ‘living without renown’ sound almost identical yet lead to opposite verdicts. The emphatic particle ஏ marks exclusivity: only the blameless truly live; the renownless are precisely the not-living. Life is thus redefined qualitatively rather than biologically. Similar ideas appear in the Talmudic teaching that the wicked are called dead even in their lifetimes, the Dhammapada’s ‘the heedless are as if dead already’, the Gita’s verdict that the self-indulgent person ‘lives in vain’, and Revelation’s church that has ‘a name that thou livest, and art dead’. Valluvar’s distinctive move is to make renown, the social trace of virtue, the test of whether one has lived at all.

tamil:
அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் பொருட்செல்வம்
பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள.
transliteration:
Arutchelvam selvaththul selvam porutchelvam,
Pooriyaar kannum ula.
current_meaning: Kindness is the richest of all riches. Money and things can be found even in the hands of the worst people.
elementary: Anyone can end up with a big pile of money, even a bully or a cheat. But a kind heart that cares about every living thing is something only good people have. So kindness is the richest treasure there is.
university: The chapter opens by reversing the ordinary hierarchy of value with a pun on selvam (wealth): arul-selvam, the wealth of grace, is ‘the wealth among wealths’, while porul-selvam, material wealth, is disqualified precisely because it is morally indiscriminate — it collects even with the pooriyaar, the base or vile. The argument is not that money is evil (Valluvar devotes the whole Book of Porul to acquiring it, and Kural 757 calls arul the child of love nursed by wealth) but that a good which the wicked can own equally well cannot be the highest good. Parimelazhagar, placing this chapter at the head of the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal), glosses arul as compassion that flows to all living beings without any tie of kinship — the matured, universalised form of the anbu (love for one’s own) praised in Chapter 8. The logic echoes Socrates’ claim that virtue is not produced by wealth, and the Stoic and Buddhist ranking of inner goods above external ones.

tamil:
நல்லாற்றாள் நாடி அருளாள்க பல்லாற்றால்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Nallaatraal naadi arulaalga pallaatraal,
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
current_meaning: Think things through the right way and make kindness your rule for living. However many ways you test it, kindness is the one thing that truly helps you.
elementary: Imagine trying every road on a map to find the safest way home. Valluvar says that whichever road you test, the one that always gets you there safely is being kind. Kindness is the friend that never lets you down.
university: The couplet is epistemological as well as ethical: naadi (having searched) and pallaatraal therinum (even if you examine by many methods) describe a process of inquiry whose result is always the same — arul is the only thunai, the companion or aid, that holds. Parimelazhagar reads pallaatraal as the conflicting doctrines of the various schools (samayams), so the kural makes a strikingly ecumenical claim: whatever creed one tests, compassion is the point on which all converge. This anticipates later comparative ethics, which often finds compassion to be the common denominator of otherwise divergent religious systems. It also sets up the chapter’s practical thesis — that arul is not one virtue among many but the reliable guide when theories disagree.

tamil:
அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க் கில்லை இருள்சேர்ந்த
இன்னா உலகம் புகல்.
transliteration:
Arulserndha nenjinaark killai irulserndha,
Innaa ulagam pugal.
current_meaning: People whose hearts are full of kindness will never enter the dark world of suffering.
elementary: Think of kindness as a lamp you carry inside you. Wherever you go, it keeps the dark away. Valluvar says people with kind hearts will never end up in the dark, sad place.
university: The couplet is built on a sound-and-image rhyme: arul serndha (joined with grace) against irul serndha (joined with darkness). Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the ‘dark world of pain’ as naragam (hell); modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as the darkness of ignorance and misery in this life. The two readings are compatible: on either view a compassionate heart is inherently protected from darkness, whether that darkness is a place one goes after death or a state one lives in now. The line compresses a moral cosmology found widely, in which a being’s inner quality decides its destination, as in the karmic ‘happy and unhappy destinations’ of the Pali canon or the Isles of the Blessed and Tartarus in Plato.

tamil:
மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லென்ப
தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை.
transliteration:
Mannuyir oambi arulaalvaarkku illenba,
Thannuyir anjum vinai.
current_meaning: Wise people say that those who protect all living things and live with kindness will never have to fear what their own actions bring back to them.
elementary: If you spend your life looking after others — feeding a stray cat, helping a friend who fell, being gentle to little creatures — you will never have to lie awake worrying about the bad things you did. Protecting others makes your own heart safe.
university: Mannuyir means ‘the enduring lives’, the whole population of living beings that fills the world, and oambi (protecting, cherishing) describes an active guardianship, not mere harmlessness. The second line allows two readings. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan take thannuyir anjum vinai as ‘evil deeds whose results one’s own soul would dread’, so the protector of life accumulates no karmic cause for fear. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it more psychologically: such a person does not fear for their own life. Either way, the kural states a principle of moral reciprocity: fearlessness is earned by protecting others. The verb enba (‘they say’) presents this as received wisdom, and it has parallels in Jain and Buddhist teaching on abhaya-dāna, the ‘gift of fearlessness’ given to all beings.

tamil:
அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை வளிவழங்கும்
மல்லன்மா ஞாலங் கரி.
transliteration:
Allal arulaalvaarkku illai valivazhangum,
Mallanmaa gnaalang kari.
current_meaning: Sorrow never comes to people who live with kindness. This great, rich earth, where the wind blows, is the proof.
elementary: Look around the whole wide world, where the wind blows over every field and sea. Valluvar says the whole world can see that kind people are not the ones who end up miserable. The earth itself is the witness.
university: Valluvar calls the whole wind-swept earth as a witness (kari), a legal image in which the world itself testifies to a moral regularity. Parimelazhagar understands the witness as the people of the world, who can see for themselves that the compassionate do not suffer. Kalaignar offers a physical metaphor instead: as the moving wind sustains the vast earth, so the inner movement of arul sustains a person through hardship. The claim, that the kind escape sorrow, is empirically bold and can be read two ways: as an external promise of protection, or as an internal truth that allal (inner affliction) cannot take root in a mind at peace with all beings. The second reading brings the kural close to the Stoic claim that genuine benevolence is invincible and to the Buddhist list of the benefits of mettā.

tamil:
பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார் என்பர் அருள்நீங்கி
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Porulneengip pochchaandhaar enbar arulneengi,
Allavai seidhozhugu vaar.
current_meaning: Wise people say that those who give up kindness and live by doing wrong have lost sight of life's real purpose and forgotten the pain they once suffered.
elementary: Imagine someone who once got badly hurt, forgets how much it hurt, and then starts hurting others. Valluvar says people who throw away kindness and do mean things have forgotten what really matters, as if they lost the map of their own life.
university: The kural turns on the word porul, which can mean ‘wealth’, ‘meaning’ or ‘the real object (of life)’. Varadarasan and Pulavar Kesikan read porul neengi as ‘having left the true end, that is, virtue’, and pochchaandhaar as ‘those who have forgotten their life’s purpose’. Parimelazhagar reads it karmically: such people neglected virtue in an earlier life and have now forgotten the sufferings it brought. Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses: they lose their wealth and also forget the pain they once endured. The unifying idea is moral amnesia. Cruelty is presented less as malice than as a forgetting, of one’s purpose and of the fellow-feeling one’s own suffering should have taught. This anticipates the reciprocal logic of Kural 250.

tamil:
அருளில்லார்க்கு அவ்வுலகம் இல்லை பொருளில்லார்க்கு
இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி யாங்கு.
transliteration:
Arulillaarkku avvulagam illai porulillaarkku,
Ivvulagam illaagi yaangu.
current_meaning: The next world has nothing for people without kindness, just as this world has nothing for people without money.
elementary: You need money to buy things in this world, like a ticket for the bus. Valluvar says kindness is the ticket for the next world. Without it, you can’t get on.
university: This is one of the Kural’s most quoted parallelisms, built on the matched pairs arul and porul (grace and wealth) and avvulagam and ivvulagam (that world and this world). It is also notably realistic: Valluvar does not pretend that poverty is irrelevant here; he concedes that this world is closed to the destitute (compare the chapter on poverty, 105). That concession makes the second claim sharper, because compassion is to be treated as the currency of the hereafter. Kalaignar gives a non-metaphysical reading: wealth is essential to the householder’s life (illaram) and compassion to the renunciate’s (thuravaram), fitting this chapter’s place at the start of the ascetic section. The couplet shows the Kural’s characteristic balance between worldly realism and spiritual priority.

tamil:
பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால் அருளற்றார்
அற்றார்மற் றாதல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Porulatraar pooppar orukaal arulatraar,
Atraarmat raadhal aridhu.
current_meaning: People who lose their money may do well again one day. But people who lose their kindness are truly poor, and they almost never get it back.
elementary: A tree can lose all its leaves in winter and still bloom again in spring. But if the tree’s roots die, it cannot grow back. Losing money is like losing leaves. Losing kindness is like losing the roots.
university: The verb pooppar, ‘they will blossom’, turns poverty into a season: the poor are like a plant between flowerings, and fortune may return orukaal, at some time. The loss of arul is described with a deliberate repetition, arul atraar atraar, ‘those bereft of grace are bereft’: they are destitute in the absolute sense, and a change in their state (maTru aadhal) is aridhu, rare or difficult. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress this asymmetry: wealth can be recovered, but compassion, once lost, rarely returns. Philosophically the kural makes a claim about character, that compassion is a root disposition and not a possession, so its loss changes who a person is rather than what they have. The word ‘rare’ rather than ‘impossible’ leaves room for moral recovery.

tamil:
தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால் தேரின்
அருளாதான் செய்யும் அறம்.
transliteration:
Therulaadhaan meypporul kandatraal therin,
Arulaadhaan seyyum aram.
current_meaning: If you look closely, the good deeds of an unkind person are like a confused person claiming to understand the deepest truth. They are not real.
elementary: Imagine someone who has never understood maths saying they solved the hardest puzzle in the book. You would not believe them. Valluvar says good deeds done by someone who does not care about others are just like that: they look right, but there is nothing real inside.
university: The comparison is carefully chosen: therulaadhaan is one whose mind is not clear, and meypporul is ultimate reality or the true meaning of scripture. Such a person may recite the words, but cannot genuinely grasp the truth. In the same way, aram (dharma, virtuous action) performed by one who does not have arul may copy the outward form (gifts, rituals, observances) without the inner substance. The kural thus makes compassion the condition of authenticity for all other virtue, a thesis found in Paul’s ‘if I have not charity’ and in the Talmudic teaching that charity is rewarded only according to the kindness in it. Kant offers a pointed contrast: he held that acts done from sympathy alone lack moral worth and that only acts done from duty have it. Valluvar’s position is closer to virtue and sentiment theorists such as Hume and Schopenhauer, for whom the motive of fellow-feeling is what makes an act good.

tamil:
வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்கதான் தன்னின்
மெலியார்மேல் செல்லு மிடத்து.
transliteration:
Valiyaarmun thannai ninaikkadhaan thannin,
Meliyaarmel sellu midaththu.
current_meaning: When you go to bully someone weaker than you, remember how you yourself felt standing scared before someone stronger than you.
elementary: Before you push around a smaller kid, remember how scared you felt when a bigger kid picked on you. That memory is a key that unlocks kindness.
university: The chapter closes with a practical technique rather than a doctrine: a deliberate act of imagination (ninaikka, ‘let him think’) timed for the moment of temptation (sellumidaththu, ‘when he goes against’). Compassion is produced by recalling one’s own vulnerability, so the powerful person is asked to see themselves in the position of the weak. This is the reflective, perspective-taking root of the Golden Rule, and it matches Aristotle’s analysis of pity (eleos) as pain at undeserved suffering that one could imagine befalling oneself. Placing this couplet last grounds the lofty arul of the opening kurals in ordinary moral psychology: universal compassion begins with a remembered fear.

tamil:
தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்குத் தான்பிறிது ஊனுண்பான்
எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்.
transliteration:
Thannoon perukkarkuth thaanpirithu oonunpaan,
Enganam aalum arul.
current_meaning: How can someone who eats another creature's flesh just to grow their own body ever be truly kind?
elementary: Imagine someone who says they love animals, but eats one just to grow bigger themselves. That doesn’t fit together, does it? This kural asks exactly that: how can you be truly kind if you make your own body grow by using up another living body?
university: The chapter opens with a rhetorical question built on a stark bodily symmetry: ஊன் (flesh) appears on both sides of the transaction — தன்னூன் (one’s own flesh) is enlarged by பிறிது ஊன் (another’s flesh). The verb ஆளும் (“rule, govern”) is telling: Valluvar does not ask whether the meat-eater can feel pity occasionally, but whether அருள் (universal compassion, the virtue of the preceding chapter 25) can be the governing principle of his life. Placed in the துறவறவியல் (the section on renunciation), the argument is addressed first to those aspiring to the ascetic ideal, though commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read it as binding on all who claim arul. The logic of feeding self at the cost of other anticipates the Mahabharata’s Anushasana Parva and Ovid’s Pythagoras almost word for word, making this one of the most cross-culturally echoed couplets in the Kural.

tamil:
பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை அருளாட்சி
ஆங்கில்லை ஊன்தின் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Porulaatchi potraathaarkku illai arulaatchi,
Aangillai oonthin pavarkku.
current_meaning: People who do not take care of their money cannot enjoy having it. In the same way, people who eat meat cannot enjoy the gift of kindness.
elementary: If you leave your bicycle out in the rain and never look after it, soon you won’t really have a bike worth riding. In the same way, if you eat animals, you can’t really keep the treasure called kindness — it slips away because you haven’t looked after it.
university: The couplet works through a precisely balanced parallel: பொருளாட்சி (the enjoyment or sovereignty of wealth) is matched with அருளாட்சி (the sovereignty of grace), and போற்றாதார் (those who do not protect) with ஊன்தின்பவர் (flesh-eaters). The comparison is instructive: wealth is not lost in a single act, but eroded by neglect; likewise compassion is not denied by one meal but hollowed out by a habit that treats life as consumable. The adverb ஆங்கு (“likewise, in that manner”) makes the analogy explicit, a typical Valluvar move from the practical sphere of porul (wealth) to the spiritual sphere of arul. The couplet thus frames compassion as a possession requiring active guarding, a theme found in Buddhist and Mahayana insistence that meat-eating corrodes karuna itself.

tamil:
படைகொண்டார் நெஞ்சம்போல் நன்னூக்காது ஒன்றன்
உடல்சுவை உண்டார் மனம்.
transliteration:
Padaikondaar nenjampol nannookkaathu ondran,
Udalsuvai undaar manam.
current_meaning: Like the heart of someone holding a weapon, the mind of someone who enjoys eating another creature's body does not turn toward goodness.
elementary: When someone is holding a sword ready to fight, they are not thinking gentle thoughts. The Kural says that someone who enjoys eating another animal’s body is in a similar mood inside — their heart is not turned toward kindness.
university: Valluvar here moves from action to psychology: the claim is about the state of the மனம் (mind) and நெஞ்சம் (heart). படைகொண்டார் — those who have taken up weapons — is a vivid image of a mind already committed to harm; the flesh-eater who has “tasted the body” (உடல்சுவை) is said to share that orientation. The key word நன்னூக்காது (“does not look toward the good”) implies a turning of attention: pleasure in flesh habituates the mind away from arul. The comparison is striking in a text that elsewhere honours warriors (Porutpaal), showing that Valluvar is describing a disposition, not condemning soldiers; it parallels the Upanishadic idea that food shapes the mind, and the Lankavatara Sutra’s claim that animals fear the meat-eater as they fear a hunter.

tamil:
அருளல்ல தியாதெனிற் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பொருளல்ல தவ்வூன் தினல்.
transliteration:
Arulalla thiyaathenir kollaamai koral,
Porulalla thavvoon thinal.
current_meaning: If you ask what kindness is and what it is not: not killing is kindness, and killing is not. Eating the flesh of what was killed is wrong.
elementary: What is kindness? Not hurting or killing. What is unkindness? Killing. So eating the meat that came from killing isn’t right either — because it depends on the unkind act.
university: This couplet has a compressed catechism structure that Parimelazhagar unpacks as: அருள் யாது? கொல்லாமை; அருளல்லது யாது? கோறல் — “What is grace? Non-killing. What is not grace? Killing.” The final clause, பொருளல்லது அவ்வூன் தினல் (“eating that flesh is not porul”), extends the moral judgement from the act of killing to the act of eating, closing the loophole that the eater is innocent because someone else killed. பொருள் here is best read as “righteousness, what is proper” (Varadarasan: அறம் அல்லாதது). The argument prefigures chapter 33 (கொல்லாமை, Non-killing), making flesh-renunciation the dietary corollary of ahimsa.

tamil:
உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை ஊனுண்ண
அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது அளறு.
transliteration:
Unnaamai ulladhu uyirnilai oonunna,
Annaaththal seyyaathu alaru.
current_meaning: Life is kept safe by not eating meat. If a person eats meat, a place of terrible suffering will swallow them and never let them out.
elementary: Many animals stay alive because people choose not to eat them. But the Kural gives a warning too: eating flesh is like falling into a deep, sticky pit that closes its mouth and won’t let you climb back out.
university: The first line, உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை, is read by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan as “the continued life of beings depends on not eating flesh,” while Karunanidhi reads it socially: because some refrain, many creatures are spared. The second line uses a vivid image: அளறு (literally “mire, bog,” conventionally “hell”) will not perform அண்ணாத்தல் — opening the mouth — to release the one it has swallowed. The mire-image suggests a moral trap from which there is no easy exit, a consequence proportional to the finality of the death inflicted. Comparable ideas of unending or long-lasting punishment for bloodshed appear in Manu’s “mamsah” etymology and in Empedocles’ exile of the blood-polluted daimon.

tamil:
தினற்பொருட்டால் கொல்லாது உலகெனின் யாரும்
விலைப்பொருட்டால் ஊன்றருவா ரில்.
transliteration:
Thinarporuttaal kollaathu ulagenin yaarum,
Vilaipporuttaal oondraruvaar il.
current_meaning: If the world did not kill animals to eat them, no one would kill animals and sell their meat for money.
elementary: Why does a shop sell something? Because people buy it. If nobody bought meat, nobody would kill animals to sell it. So the person who buys is part of the reason the animal was killed.
