university: This is the most analytical couplet of the chapter, and it answers a specific excuse: “I did not kill; I only bought meat already killed.” Valluvar identifies the causal chain — தினற்பொருட்டு (for the sake of eating) generates விலைப்பொருட்டு (for the sake of price) — so that the consumer’s demand is the root cause of the butcher’s act. G. U. Pope’s translation makes the rebuttal explicit (“Who’d kill and sell, I pray, if none came there the flesh to buy?”). The argument is strikingly modern, anticipating demand-side ethics, and directly contests the Theravada allowance of meat not seen, heard or suspected to be killed for oneself; it closely matches Manu 5.51, which counts the buyer among the slayers.

tamil:
உண்ணாமை வேண்டும் புலாஅல் பிறிதொன்றன்
புண்ணது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Unnaamai vendum pulaaal pirithondran,
Punnathu unarvaarp perin.
current_meaning: If people understood that meat is really the wound of another living creature, they would stop eating it.
elementary: If you saw a hurt animal with a sore, you would never want to eat that sore. The Kural says meat is really just that — a wound cut from another living creature. If we remembered that, we wouldn’t want to eat it.
university: The force of the couplet lies in a single noun, புண் (wound, sore, ulcer). By renaming meat as “another creature’s wound,” Valluvar strips away the culinary vocabulary that disguises its origin, a technique of moral re-description. The conditional உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (“if one gains those who perceive / if one comes to perceive”) makes the argument depend on clear perception: the problem is not ignorance of a rule but a failure to see what is in front of us. The metrical lengthening in புலாஅல் (alapedai) lingers on the word “flesh,” as if forcing the reader to look at it. Plutarch and Ovid’s Pythagoras make the very same move, calling meat “sores” and “pitiful wounds.”

tamil:
செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார் உண்ணார்
உயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த ஊன்.
transliteration:
Seyirin thalaippirindha kaatchiyaar unnaar,
Uyirin thalaippirindha oon.
current_meaning: People who see clearly, free of confusion and fault, will not eat the flesh of a body that has lost its life.
elementary: When your eyes are clear, you see things as they really are. People whose minds are clear and free from wrong ideas look at meat and see a body that was once alive — so they don’t eat it.
university: The couplet is built on an elegant repetition: தலைப்பிரிந்த (“separated from”) occurs in both lines — the wise are separated from செயிர் (fault, delusion), while the flesh is separated from உயிர் (life). The parallel suggests a moral symmetry: purity of vision is achieved by the same act of separation that, done to a living being, produces flesh. காட்சியார் (“those of vision”) links the virtue to perception, continuing kural 257’s theme that seeing clearly ends the desire for meat. Parimelazhagar glosses செயிர் as the delusion (mayakkam) that makes one mistake the body for the self, placing this couplet within the ascetic epistemology of the துறவறவியல்.

tamil:
அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின் ஒன்றன்
உயிர்செகுத் துண்ணாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Avisorindh thaayiram vettalin ondran,
Uyirsekuth thunnaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Not killing a single creature to eat it is better than making a thousand offerings by pouring butter into a holy fire.
elementary: Some people think doing big, fancy religious ceremonies makes them very good. The Kural says: sparing just one animal’s life, and not eating it, is better than a thousand of those ceremonies.
university: This couplet makes a pointed comparison with Vedic ritual: அவி (havis, oblations such as ghee) poured into the fire in a thousand வேள்வி (yajñas, sacrifices). By ranking the simple restraint of not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices, Valluvar subordinates ritual merit to ethical conduct — a critique shared with the Jain and Buddhist movements and with the later Upanishadic interiorisation of sacrifice. The numerical contrast (ஆயிரம் versus ஒன்றன் — “a thousand” versus “one”) is characteristic of Valluvar’s rhetoric of disproportion. Manu 5.53 offers a strikingly similar valuation, equating lifelong abstention from meat with a century of horse-sacrifices, while the Hebrew prophets and Jesus prefer “mercy, and not sacrifice.”

tamil:
கொல்லான் புலாலை மறுத்தானைக் கைகூப்பி
எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும்.
transliteration:
Kollaan pulaalai maruththaanaik kaikooppi,
Ellaa uyirum thozhum.
current_meaning: All living creatures will put their hands together and honor the one who does not kill and refuses to eat meat.
elementary: Imagine every animal in the world putting its paws together to say “thank you” to one person. That’s the picture here: the person who never kills and never eats animals is loved and honoured by every living thing.
university: The chapter closes with an image of cosmic reverence: எல்லா உயிரும் (all living beings) perform கைகூப்பித் தொழுதல் — the joined-palm gesture of worship. The two qualifications, கொல்லான் (one who does not kill) and புலாலை மறுத்தான் (one who has refused flesh), sum up the chapter and anticipate the next section on கொல்லாமை. The hyperbole of animals folding hands is deliberate: the one who renounces power over other lives receives from them the honour usually given to gods. Parallel visions appear in Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, Empedocles’ age when “all things were tame and gentle to man,” and the Buddhist teaching that one who cultivates goodwill is dear to human and non-human beings alike.

tamil:
உற்றநோய் நோன்றல் உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை
அற்றே தவத்திற் குரு.
transliteration:
Utra noi nondral uyirkku urukan seyyaamai
Atre thavaththirku uru.
current_meaning: Patiently bearing the pain that comes to you, and never hurting any other living thing: this is what true penance (a life of strict self-control) really is.
elementary: Imagine someone bumps into you and it hurts. Penance, says Valluvar, is two simple things: you put up with the hurt without making a fuss, and you never hurt anyone back or hurt anyone at all. That is what being a real ‘tapas’ person looks like.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition that is striking for what it leaves out: no fire rituals, no fasting regimens, no forest hermitage, only a two-part ethical formula — endurance (நோன்றல், noṉṟal) of suffering that befalls oneself, and non-infliction (செய்யாமை) of suffering on other lives. The emphatic அற்றே (‘just that much’) deliberately reduces tapas from spectacle to disposition. Parimelazhagar notes that the suffering endured includes both what arises naturally (hunger, cold, illness) and what others inflict, which aligns the verse closely with the Jain and Buddhist redefinition of austerity as patience plus ahiṃsā. The move is thus both conservative (it keeps the prestigious word ‘tapas’) and reformist (it ethicizes it), and it frames every later claim in the chapter about the ‘power’ of tapas as resting on this moral foundation.

tamil:
தவமும் தவமுடையார்க்கு ஆகும் அதனை
அஃதிலார் மேற்கொள் வது.
transliteration:
Thavamum thavamudaiyaarkku aagum adhanai
Aqdhilaar merkolvadhu.
current_meaning: Penance (a life of strict self-control) works only for those who truly have its inner strength. For others, just going through the motions of it is useless.
elementary: Wearing a doctor’s coat does not make you a doctor. In the same way, putting on the clothes and habits of a holy person does not work unless you really have the patience and goodness inside.
university: The couplet turns on a pun-like repetition: தவம் (tapas) comes only to those who have தவம். Commentators split on what the second ‘tapas’ means. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it karmically — only those who accumulated tapas in earlier births can undertake it now — while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as a warning against தவக்கோலம், the ascetic costume adopted without ascetic conduct. The second reading anticipates the very next chapter, கூடாவொழுக்கம் (‘Imposture’), and fits Valluvar’s habitual suspicion of form without substance. Either way, the verse asserts that tapas is not a technique anyone can pick up but the outward expression of an already-formed inner capacity.

tamil:
துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி மறந்தார்கொல்
மற்றை யவர்கள் தவம்.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarkku thuppuravu vendi marandhaarkol
Matraiyavargal thavam.
current_meaning: Is it because others wanted to give food and help to the people who gave up the world that they forgot to practice self-control themselves?
elementary: Picture a whole village cooking lunch for a few hermits on the hill. Valluvar jokes: maybe everyone got so busy packing lunches for the hermits that they forgot to become good and disciplined themselves!
university: This is one of Valluvar’s rare ironic rhetorical questions (கொல் marks doubt). Read straightforwardly, it offers an indulgent explanation for why so few undertake tapas: society needs householders to feed the ascetics. Read more sharply — as Kalaignar does — it is a rebuke: supporting renunciants is no substitute for one’s own discipline. The verse also documents a real economic structure of early Indian religion, in which Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical renouncers depended on lay donation, and in which donors believed they shared the merit of those they supported. Valluvar gently punctures the complacency that such a division of spiritual labour could produce.

tamil:
ஒன்னார்த் தெறலும் உவந்தாரை ஆக்கலும்
எண்ணின் தவத்தான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Onnaar theralum uvandhaarai aakkalum
Ennin thavaththaan varum.
current_meaning: If a person who practices strict self-control wishes it, that power alone can defeat enemies and lift up friends.
elementary: In old stories, people who did very long and sincere penance got special powers — like a superhero who trained for years. Valluvar says such a person could, just by wishing it, stop bad people and help good friends.
university: Here Valluvar adopts the widespread Indian belief that tapas generates real, even cosmic, power — the power to curse (சாபம்) and to bless (அருள்), as Parimelazhagar glosses ஆற்றல் in the neighbouring verse. The conditional எண்ணின் (‘if he wills’) is crucial: after 261 defined the ascetic as one who harms no one, the implication is that such power exists but is normally left unused. The verse thus holds a tension typical of Indian ascetic literature, where rishis like Vishvamitra or Durvasa possess destructive capacity that their own ethic ought to restrain. Modern commentators such as Kalaignar demythologize it as the practical power of resolve and self-control.

tamil:
வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்
ஈண்டு முயலப் படும்.
transliteration:
Vendiya vendiyaangu eydhalaal seydhavam
Eendu muyalap padum.
current_meaning: Strict self-control lets a person get whatever they want, just as they want it. So it should be worked at with effort, here and now.
elementary: If you practise the piano every day, one day you can play any song you want, just the way you want. Valluvar says tapas is like that for your whole life — so start practising now, not later.
university: The verse gives the motivational logic of tapas: it is effective, delivering desired ends ‘as desired’ (வேண்டியாங்கு). ஈண்டு (‘here’) is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in this birth’, urging urgency, while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘even in the householder’s state’, democratizing tapas beyond the forest. The claim sits in tension with the Gita’s ideal of desireless action and with Valluvar’s own later chapter on the destruction of desire (அவா அறுத்தல்); commentators resolve this by noting that for the truly austere the highest ‘desire’ is liberation itself. The couplet thus captures tapas at its most instrumental while quietly pointing beyond instrumentality.

tamil:
தவஞ்செய்வார் தங்கருமஞ் செய்வார்மற் றல்லார்
அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Thavanjeyvaar thangarumanj seyvaar matru allaar
Avanjeyvaar aasaiyut pattu.
current_meaning: People who practice strict self-control are doing their own true work. Everyone else is caught in the trap of wanting things and only works toward their own harm.
elementary: Think of a fly stuck in a spider’s web — the more it wriggles, the more stuck it gets. Valluvar says people who chase every want are like that fly, while people who practise self-control are doing the one job that really helps them.
university: The couplet rests on a sonic antithesis — தவம் (tavam, penance) against அவம் (avam, futility or self-harm) — so that tapas and its absence differ by a single consonant. தம் கருமம் (‘their own work’) implies that spiritual self-cultivation is a person’s genuine duty, while the ‘busy’ worldly life is in fact a failure to act for oneself. Parimelazhagar glosses அவம் as bringing harm upon oneself, since desire-driven action produces karmic bondage. The verse inverts ordinary valuations: the ascetic who seems idle is the only one truly working, and the striving householder, if driven by desire, is idle in the deepest sense.
